character.name: Ines Calder
character.sheet: Ines Calder, 38, the only doctor in Kessel Pass, a mountain railway town where a new tunnel is being driven through the ridge. Trained as a ship's surgeon; came inland six years ago after a patient, the boy Petr Anko, died under her knife in the old clinic. Blunt, tired, funny when she forgets to be careful, keeps meticulous case notes. Estranged from her younger sister Lotte for nine years over their mother's will. Drive: that no one in her care dies of something she could have seen coming.

memories.experienced: Sanna had the stove lit before I came down at seven, as she does every morning, and the waiting bench already held three people coughing in three different keys. Frost on the inside of the surgery window. Old Frau Lechner had the same dry cough she has had since August and wanted it to be something interesting. The carter's boy had a wet one that rattled on the left. Sanna told me the carbolic was down to half a bottle and that the kettle handle had come loose again.
memories.did: I listened to all three chests, told Frau Lechner it was the stove smoke and not consumption, and told her twice because she did not believe me the first time. I sent the carter's boy home with a mustard plaster and orders to stay out of the yard for four days. I tightened the kettle handle with the small screwdriver from the instrument drawer and burned my thumb doing it. I wrote carbolic on the slate by the door so Sanna would stop reminding me.

memories.experienced: Otto Brandt carried his daughter in at half past ten with flour still on his forearms. Mila is nine and small for it. She had walked up the hill and could not get her breath back; I heard the wheeze from across the room before I had the stethoscope out. Both bases tight, a whistle on the out-breath, lips a shade too blue at the edges. Otto said she had been helping at the bakehouse since five, sifting, because his wife has her bad back again.
memories.did: I sat Mila upright on the couch, opened the window a crack despite Sanna's face, and had her breathe steam from a basin with a towel over her head for ten minutes. When the wheeze eased I told Otto, plainly, that flour dust in the air was feeding it and that she was to be kept out of the bakehouse while they sifted. He said, 'Then who sifts?' I said, 'Not her.' I entered her in my casebook, page for the Brandts, with the date and 'wheeze, flour dust, lips dusky at rest'.

memories.experienced: At the pharmacy for carbolic, Grete Ammer served me herself, pleasant as ever, then slid a folded note across the counter with the bottle. In her careful hand: 'Doctor Calder -- account overdue since midsummer, 186 crowns. With respect, G. Ammer.' Behind her the big green ledger lay open, and I could see my name at the top of a column that ran most of the way down the page. A carter was waiting behind me and heard the paper crackle.
memories.did: I put the note in my coat pocket without reading it twice, which was a lie to myself, because I had read it twice. I told Grete I had fees coming in at the end of the month and would bring something before then. She said, 'I know you will, Doctor,' which was worse than if she had been sharp. I paid cash for the carbolic, one crown twenty, and walked home the long way so I would not have to go past the bank.

memories.experienced: Supper was bread, the end of the cheese and a boiled egg eaten standing up in the kitchen above the surgery. The wind came down off the ridge and rattled the loose pane. At nine the tunnel blasting started, as it does most nights now: a dull thump I felt in the floorboards more than heard, then the cups on the dresser ticking against each other. Two more after it, eleven minutes apart. The street was empty; only one window across the square was still lit.
memories.did: I wedged the loose pane with a folded page of old newspaper and moved the cups to the back of the shelf so they would stop talking. I counted the gap between blasts on my watch out of habit, the way I used to count between contractions, and wondered how many men were up at the heading at this hour and how many of them I would be stitching by Christmas. Then I went to bed with my stockings on and did not sleep until after the third.

memories.experienced: The Weber boy hammered on my door at a quarter to three: his mother's waters had gone. Sanna was already there when I arrived in the lower town, sleeves rolled, water on. Frau Weber's fourth, a girl, came at ten past five, cord once round the neck and slipped off easily, cried loud enough to wake the street. The afterbirth was complete. Herr Weber, who had been in the yard the whole time, asked if it was a boy three times before he believed us.
memories.did: I checked the placenta twice on the kitchen table under the lamp, because I always do. I told Herr Weber, 'Girl. Healthy. Stop asking.' I left Sanna to wash and settle the mother and walked home in the grey light with my bag, and on the way I said out loud to nobody that it was a good night's work, which is the kind of thing you only say when no one can hear. I charged them two crowns and knew I would get one.

memories.experienced: Mid-morning a big man in a good wool coat walked in holding a young navvy by the elbow. He said he was Konrad Voss, chief engineer for the contractor. The boy, Pauli Hass, nineteen, had his left middle finger crushed between a rail and a skip at the tunnel mouth: the tip pulped, nail gone, bone showing. Voss watched me work without flinching and said the company would rather settle directly than through its books. He put twenty-five crowns in notes on my desk.
memories.did: I cleaned the finger, took off the crushed tip at the last joint and closed it with four stitches, and told Pauli he would keep the rest of it if he kept it dry. I said to Voss, 'Twenty-five is too much for a fingertip.' He said, 'Then it covers the next one.' I took the notes because I needed them and hated that he could see I did. I entered the case in my casebook as 'crush, rail and skip, tunnel mouth, paid by K. Voss, cash', and underlined cash.

memories.experienced: Grete's shop smelled of camphor and wet coats. She looked up from the counter and saw the notes in my hand before I said anything. She opened the green ledger, found my column, and ran her finger down it. Her spectacles were pushed up in her hair and she had to hunt for them. She said the price of quinine from the city had gone up again this autumn and she did not know how the camp would manage if anything went through it.
memories.did: I put twenty of Voss's crowns on the counter and asked her to write it against my account. She wrote '20 -- paid, Dr. C.' in the ledger and turned the book round so I could see the new balance: 166 crowns. I said, 'There. I am slightly less of a disgrace.' She laughed and said I was no disgrace, only a doctor. I kept the other five for coal. I did not ask about the quinine price, which I should have.

memories.experienced: Past eleven, a knock at the side door. A man in a work jacket, thirties, soot in the creases of his neck, holding his right hand against his chest wrapped in a rag. The palm and the insides of three fingers were blistered and weeping, a narrow burn across the base like a line drawn with something hot. He smelled of black powder and tallow. He said he had burned it on a stove. When I asked his name he said, 'Put down a man. I'll pay.'
memories.did: I cut the blisters clean, dressed the palm with lint and carron oil and bound the fingers separately so they would not heal together. I told him that was no stove burn, that stoves burn the back of the hand when you reach over them, not a line across the palm. He said nothing. I told him to come back in two days so I could change the dressing and look for pus. He paid with a crown piece and left by the side door. I wrote him in the casebook as 'unknown man, burn right palm, fuse?'

memories.experienced: Sanna found the used dressings in the bin when she came in at seven and asked who had come in the night. She has a way of asking that means she already knows it was not in the day book. Rain on the windows all morning. A woman came for a tonic for her husband that I suspect was for her. The casebook lay open on the desk where I had left it, the ink of last night's entry smudged where my cuff had dragged across it.
memories.did: I told Sanna, 'A man with a burned hand who would not say who he was.' She said, 'From the tunnel,' and I said, 'Probably. He smelled of powder.' I re-inked the smudged entry, 'unknown man, burn right palm, fuse?', and added 'refused name; paid 1 cr.; to return Thursday.' I gave the tonic woman iron and told her to eat meat on Sundays, and to sit down more, which she laughed at.

memories.experienced: The bakery was warm and fogged, and Mila was behind the counter, not in the bakehouse, which I noticed with satisfaction. She was folding paper bags and coughing into her elbow the way I showed her last spring. Otto was in the back; I could hear the sieve going. Mila told me her chest was 'only a bit squeaky today'. She gave me the end of a rye loaf I had not asked for and said her father said doctors never eat.
memories.did: I bought a rye loaf and two poppy rolls, forty heller, and put my ear to Mila's back right there by the counter while she held her breath and giggled. Still a whistle on the left, less than yesterday. I called through to Otto that she was to stay out front until the sifting was done every day, not just today, and he shouted back, 'Yes, Doctor, yes.' I ate one poppy roll walking up the hill and felt the cold go into my teeth.

memories.experienced: Old Herr Pichler on Tanner Street had his gout back in the right big toe, the joint red and shining like a plum. He had been drinking the new wine from the valley and denied it with a bottle on the windowsill. His cat sat on my bag the whole time. The rain turned to sleet halfway through the visit and the gutter outside his window began to run like a tap.
memories.did: I told him the wine or the toe, pick one. He picked the wine, as he does every October. I left him colchicum drops, ten at night, and wrote the dose on the back of an envelope because he loses paper. I lifted the cat off my bag twice and the third time took the bag with the cat on it to the door, which made him laugh so hard the toe hurt. He paid me in eggs, six, wrapped in a stocking.

memories.experienced: The quickest way back from Tanner Street is down Mill Lane, and the sleet made me take it. The old surgery is still there on the left past the ropemaker, shutters nailed, the brass plate taken down but the four screw holes still in the stone where it hung. Someone has put a cart against the door. I could smell wet plaster. A child was bouncing a ball against the side wall, and the thud of it went on behind me all the way to the corner.
memories.did: I kept my eyes on the cobbles and walked on the far side of the lane, which is what I always do. I did not look up at the second window, the operating room, where the light was good in the mornings. I counted my steps to the corner, forty-two, because counting keeps the Anko boy's face out of it, mostly. At the corner I found I had cracked one of Pichler's eggs in my fist. I wiped my glove on the wall and went home.

memories.experienced: At four Frau Maier brought in her Jonas, seven, who had come off the ropewalk wall and opened his knee on the edge of a stone step. A clean flap, gravel in it, blood in his sock. He was being very brave and very loud about how brave he was. Sanna held his shoulders and told him about her brother who fell off a roof and grew up to be a policeman, which I am fairly sure she invented on the spot.
memories.did: I picked the gravel out with forceps, washed it with carbolic, and put in three stitches while Jonas counted them aloud and got to five. I told him he could tell his friends it was six. I gave him a barley sugar from the jar I keep for exactly this. His mother asked what she owed and I said, 'Half a crown, when you have it,' and wrote it down in the casebook, knowing it would sit there until spring.

memories.experienced: I went down to the station at noon to collect the crate from the city supply house: lint, catgut, carbolic, and two tins of quinine powders, twenty-five to a tin. Emil Ott came out of his office before I reached the parcels window, cap on, looking pleased to have news first. He said, 'Doctor, your sister got off the 11:20. Calder, she said, asking for you. A woman and a little girl, dark plait, blue coat. Two trunks. I sent them to the Hart.'
memories.did: I said, 'My sister is in the city.' Ott said, 'Not since the 11:20 she isn't.' I signed for the crate and checked the quinine tins against the invoice, both of them, because my hands wanted something to do. I asked him whether she had looked well. He said she had looked tired, and the girl had not said a word the whole time on the platform. I asked him to have the crate carried up to the clinic and stood on the platform for a minute after he had gone back in.

memories.experienced: The afternoon patients came and went: a farmer's split thumb, a girl with nits, the knife-grinder's rheumatism. Sanna unpacked the crate and put the quinine tins on the high shelf. I kept hearing my mother's lawyer reading in his office nine years ago, and Lotte standing up so fast her chair went over when he came to the garnet brooch. Sanna asked me twice whether I wanted the nit comb boiled and I did not hear her the first time.
memories.did: I treated all three and got the nits wrong, handing the paraffin to the mother with instructions for her own hair instead of the girl's, and had to call her back from the door. I told Sanna, 'My sister is in town,' and she said, 'You have a sister?' I said, 'Apparently.' I closed the surgery at half past five, half an hour early, washed my face, and changed my collar, and was annoyed with myself for changing my collar.

memories.experienced: Lotte was in the Hart's back parlour by the fire. Nine years older and thinner, her good city coat worn at the cuffs, her hair up the way our mother wore it. She stood when I came in and did not come forward. She said, 'Ines.' I said, 'Lotte.' That was most of it. She said they needed somewhere for a while. When I asked where Friedrich was she said, 'Busy,' and then, 'Don't,' before I had asked anything else.
memories.did: I sat down across the table because standing felt like a quarrel. I told her the Hart was clean and the landlady fair, and that my rooms above the clinic were small but she could have them if she wanted. She said the Hart would do. I asked how long 'a while' was; she said she did not know. I said, 'Is he coming after you?' and she looked at the fire and said, 'I said don't.' I paid for their supper at the bar on my way out without telling her.

memories.experienced: The girl was Mira, eight. She sat on the settle beside the fire with a cloth rabbit missing one ear, and she has Lotte's chin and our father's eyes, which was a thing I was not ready for. When Lotte said, 'This is your Aunt Ines,' she looked at me the way you look at a dog you have been told is friendly. She did not answer anything I said. When I held out my hand she turned her face into Lotte's skirt.
memories.did: I crouched down to her height, which my knees objected to, and said, 'Hello, Mira. I am the doctor here. I mend people.' Nothing. I took a peppermint from my coat pocket and put it on the settle beside the rabbit instead of holding it out to her. I said, 'That is for the rabbit, if he wants it.' When I looked back from the door the peppermint was gone, and she was still not looking at me.

memories.experienced: Back at the clinic the rooms seemed bigger and colder than they had that morning. The midnight blast came from the ridge and the cups ticked. I kept seeing Lotte's hands, which she had kept in her lap under the table the whole time, and the two trunks Ott had mentioned. Nobody brings two trunks for a visit. Nobody brings a child up a mountain in October for a visit, either, not to a sister she has not written to in nine years.
memories.did: I sat at the kitchen table with a cup of cold tea and wrote on the back of an envelope what I knew: two trunks, no husband, 'busy', 'don't', the girl silent. Then I crossed it out because it looked like a case note, and she is not a case. I thought about the brooch, which the will gave to her and which I have not laid eyes on in nine years, and wondered whether it had come up the mountain in one of those trunks. I went to bed at one.

memories.experienced: Father Kurz caught me at the church gate on my way to the Lechners. He had heard already, of course. The Hart's kitchen girl had told his housekeeper that the doctor's sister came with two trunks, a child, and no husband, and had asked the landlady for the weekly rate, not the nightly. He wanted to know whether Herr Calder -- he assumed the name -- would be joining them. He said it kindly. He always says it kindly.
memories.did: I told him my sister's married name was not Calder, and that her husband was in the city, which as far as I knew was true. He asked if I would bring them to Mass on Sunday so the parish could make them welcome. I said I would ask, and that the parish could make them welcome without knowing their business first. He laughed and patted my arm and said, 'Ines, the parish IS its business.' I went on to the Lechners and was short with Frau Lechner, who did not deserve it.

memories.end: worried in a low, practical way
memories.experienced: Friday is Sanna's scrubbing day: every instrument boiled, every shelf wiped, the floor done with soda. While she scrubbed she read me the stock off the shelves. Lint, plenty. Catgut, two packets. Carbolic, one bottle and the new one. Quinine: the two new tins and the dregs of an old one, fifty-three powders in all. She said that was not much if the camp had a bad winter, and that the last bad winter the powders had gone in a fortnight.
memories.did: I wrote the counts on the slate: lint, catgut, carbolic, 'quinine 53'. I told Sanna fifty-three powders would see us through anything short of an epidemic, and she said, 'And if it is not short of one?' I said then we would buy more, and we both knew I meant from Grete, on credit I no longer really have. I moved the quinine from the high shelf to the locked cupboard, and put the key on my watch chain.

memories.experienced: A tall man with spectacles and ink on his right cuff came in at three and said the school board required him to have a certificate of health before he started on Monday. Teodor Lind, the new schoolteacher, off the morning train from the lowlands with a box of books and a cold. He apologised for the cold, for the books, for taking my time. He asked whether it was true the children here learn their letters from the railway timetables. He was entirely serious.
memories.did: I listened to his chest, which was sound, looked at his throat, which was red, and wrote him a certificate stating he was 'fit to teach, if not to talk'. He read it and laughed out loud, and I was pleased with myself for longer than it deserved. I told him the schoolhouse stove smoked and to leave the top door of it open. He asked my name twice, the second time, I think, to be sure of it. I did not charge him.

memories.experienced: I ate supper with them at the Hart, Lotte's invitation, sent by the kitchen girl on a scrap of paper: 'Supper at 7 if you like. L.' Mutton stew, too salty. Lotte asked about schooling for Mira, practically, as if we were acquaintances. Mira ate with her head down and drew houses in the margin of an old newspaper with a stub of pencil, all with smoke coming out of the chimneys. Once, when I laughed at something, she glanced up at me and away.
memories.did: I told Lotte the new schoolteacher had arrived that morning and seemed decent, 'polite to the point of illness', and that I would take them to meet him on Sunday. Lotte said, 'Thank you,' formally. I asked Mira whether the houses were ours, here in town. She did not answer, but she drew a second, taller house next to the first with a red cross on the door, and pushed the paper an inch toward me. I did not touch it, in case it was not meant.

memories.experienced: Saturday market in the square, sun on the frost. At the egg stall, not two yards from me, stood Marta Anko, greyer than last year, a basket on her arm. She saw me. I saw her see me. She put back the eggs she was holding, turned her back, and walked off toward the fountain without buying anything. The egg woman looked at me and then very hard at her eggs. Somebody behind me said, 'Six years,' not quite under their breath.
memories.did: I stood where I was and bought a dozen eggs I did not need, since I still had Pichler's. I did not follow her or call out. Six years ago I said everything I had to say at her door and she shut it, and there is nothing new. I paid, thanked the egg woman, and walked the other way round the fountain so as not to cross her again. The whole way I could feel the weight of the boy on the table, which is absurd, since I never carried him.

memories.experienced: The rest of the market was ordinary and I was grateful for it. Apples from the valley, small and hard. The cheese woman's goitre was bigger; she asked if I thought it was the water. Snow had come down the ridge in the night as far as the tree line and the spoil heaps looked grey against it. A dog stole a sausage from the butcher's board and the butcher chased it into a doorway shouting.
memories.did: I bought two pounds of apples, a wedge of mountain cheese and a new wick for the kitchen lamp. I told the cheese woman it was not the water, it was iodine she lacked, and to buy salt fish when the carter brought it. I laughed at the dog along with everyone else, which helped. I carried it all home in my bag with the eggs on top, and made an apple cake for the first time since spring, badly.

memories.experienced: In the afternoon a boy came down from the camp to fetch me for a man who had turned his ankle on the spoil and could not walk. The bunkhouses below the portal were mud to the ankles and smelled of wet wool and fried onions. From there you can hear the drills at the tunnel face, a steady chatter coming out of the ridge. The upper well by the spoil heap, above bunkhouse two, had a tin cup on a chain; the water was clear and very cold.
memories.did: I strapped the ankle, a bad sprain and not a break, and told the man a week off it. He laughed and said the company would dock him the week. I drank a cup from the upper well because I was thirsty after the climb, and told the cook his onions were the best thing I had smelled all week, which got me a plate of them. I looked up at the portal on the way down and counted the men going in on the shift change: twenty-two.

memories.experienced: Saturday evening Sanna goes to her mother's in the valley, so the clinic was quiet. I did the week in the casebook: twenty-nine patients, one birth, one crushed finger, one burned hand of no name. When I added up what I had actually been paid, it came to thirty-eight crowns, eggs and the Maier half-crown not counted. Grete's note was still in my coat pocket; I found it when I went to hang the coat up.
memories.did: I wrote the week's total at the foot of the casebook page, 'paid 38 cr.', and under it, smaller, 'Grete 166'. I put Grete's note in the casebook as a bookmark so I would stop finding it in pockets. I made a plan: ten crowns to her by the ninth, the rest from the contractor's fees if it paid its bills, and I wrote her a line saying so. Then I ate a slab of the bad apple cake standing at the window and went to bed early.

memories.experienced: Mass at St. Veit's, cold enough to see breath. Lotte and Mira came, and sat at the back; half the parish turned round to look at them. Father Kurz preached on the prodigal son, which I am almost certain was aimed. Afterwards he stood at the door and introduced the new schoolteacher to everyone as they came out. Teodor's cold was worse. When he saw me he said, 'Fit to teach, if not to talk,' in a croak, and grinned.
memories.did: I sat with Lotte and Mira at the back instead of my usual pew, so that nobody would have the satisfaction of seeing us apart. I told Father Kurz at the door that the sermon was very pointed, and he said, 'Was it?' I introduced Lotte and Mira to Teodor. I told him to gargle salt water, and he said he would if I promised not to charge him again. I said I had not charged him the first time. He said that was why he had noticed.

memories.experienced: Teodor walked us to the schoolhouse after Mass to enrol Mira. It is one room, twenty-three desks, a stove that smokes, a map of the Empire with a tear through the mountains. He opened a register and asked Mira her name and age. She answered him straight off: 'Mira. Eight. Nine in March.' Five words, to a stranger, in a clear voice. She had not said one to me in three days. He wrote her down and gave her the desk by the window.
memories.did: I stood by the stove with Lotte and watched, and felt jealous of a schoolteacher, which I noted and did not enjoy. I opened the stove's top door for him, as I had told him to. I told Mira the desk by the window was the best one, because you could see the trains. She did not answer me, but she looked at the window. On the walk back Lotte said, 'She likes him.' I said, 'Everybody likes him. It is infuriating.' Lotte very nearly laughed.

memories.experienced: I walked up the path above town in the afternoon because it was fine and I had nothing to stitch. From the bend by the wayside shrine you can see the whole ridge: the new tunnel portal with its timber mouth and the spoil tipped below it, and higher up, the black adits of the old silver workings, three of them, like missing teeth. A kestrel hung over the old spoil. The drills had stopped for Sunday and the valley was so quiet I could hear the river.
memories.did: I sat on the shrine step and ate an apple and looked at the two holes in the mountain, the old and the new, and thought how close together they seemed from down here. I asked a shepherd coming down whether anyone went into the old workings any more; he said only fools and goats. I told him I would keep out, then. I walked back down before the light went, stiff in the knees and pleased with the day.

memories.experienced: At ten a navvy was brought in by two friends with his eyebrow split to the bone from a bottle at the Hart, very drunk, very cheerful, blood all down his shirt. While I stitched him the friends argued about whose round it had been. When they had gone I went through the casebook for the week and came again to the entry for the man with the burned hand. He had been told to come back on Thursday. It was Sunday. He had not come.
memories.did: I put five stitches in the eyebrow and told him if he pulled them out I would put them back without cleaning the needle, which sobered him slightly. I charged the friends a crown between them and got it. Then I sat with the casebook and wrote beside the burned-hand entry: 'did not return; watch for infection; if seen, find his name.' I thought of Lotte and Mira at the Hart, two streets away, and of the peppermint that had disappeared. I locked the side door and went up.

memories.experienced: At half past six Sanna let in the man with the burned hand, the one who came at night last week and would not give a name. He was grey and sweating. The dressing I put on him was black with dirt and the right palm under it was swollen tight, red streaks running up past the wrist, pus under the blister roof. His skin was hot to the back of my hand and his pulse ran at a hundred and eight. He said, "It went bad on Friday. I kept working."
memories.did: I told him he was an idiot and sat him down before he fell down. I said I would not touch the hand until he gave me a name, because I do not open infected palms on ghosts. He said, "Anton Reis. Shot-firer, north gang." I wrote it on a fresh card. Sanna boiled the lancet and the basin while I cut the old dressing away, and I told him plainly that if the red went past the elbow he could lose the hand, and he would lose it at my table, not the company's.

memories.experienced: Anton held still while I lanced it; he only swore once, in a language I did not know. A good cupful of pus came out. To keep his mind off it he talked about the work: he sets and fires the charges at the heading, and before every shift the foreman takes the firedamp readings and writes them in the book. He said, "Funny thing, Doctor. The readings come out the same every shift. Point four. Always point four. Rock doesn't do that."
memories.did: I packed the wound with carbolic lint, bound the hand in a sling and gave him willow bark for the fever. I asked him who reads the lamps. He said Stoll keeps the gas log himself and nobody else touches it. I said, "And you're telling a doctor instead of the inspector?" He said a doctor doesn't have a foreman. That night I wrote in my casebook: A. Reis, 31, shot-firer, infected burn R palm, lanced. Under it, smaller: 'readings same every shift - 0.4'. I don't know why I wrote that part down, except that I write everything down.

memories.experienced: The afternoon was ordinary and I was grateful. Old Frau Weiss came with her leg ulcer, which smelled better than last week. A carter had a splinter in his thumb the length of a matchstick and was proud of it. It rained all afternoon, thin cold rain off the ridge, and the waiting-room stove smoked whenever the wind turned. Sanna brought up barley soup at two and complained that the coal merchant had put his price up again by a heller a sack.
memories.did: I dressed the ulcer with zinc paste and told Frau Weiss to keep the leg up, which she will not do. I pulled the carter's splinter in one piece and gave it to him in a twist of paper because he asked for it. I ate the soup standing at the window. I told Sanna the coal man could put his price up all he liked, we were burning the old chair next week if we had to. She said she would hold me to it.

memories.experienced: Supper at the Hart with Lotte and Mira, the third time since they came. The landlady gave us the corner table by the fire and a mutton stew. Lotte talked about the weather and the trains and nothing else. Mira sat with her plate and ate the potatoes one by one and did not look up once. When I asked her if she liked the school, she looked at her mother, not at me. Lotte said, "She likes Herr Lind. She says he has a dog."
memories.did: I said Herr Lind's dog was a disgrace and had once eaten a bandage off my own ankle, which is true. Mira did not laugh but her fork stopped. I asked Lotte, carefully, how long they meant to stay at the Hart, since the rooms are dear. She said, "We'll see," and poured more water. I paid for the three suppers, one crown twenty, which I could not afford, and walked home in the rain wondering what exactly my sister had left in the city that she would not name.

memories.experienced: Before the bakery opened I went round the back to see Mila Brandt. The kitchen was hot with the first ovens and white with flour. Mila was sitting on a sack, nine years old and thin as a rake handle, coughing the loose cough that comes up in the mornings. Her right base crackled under the stethoscope, same as last week, not worse. Otto Brandt stood in the doorway with his arms floury to the elbow and asked if it was the flour dust.
memories.did: I told Otto the flour dust does her no favours and she should sleep in the front room, away from the ovens, until the thaw. I showed Mila how to lean over a basin of hot water with a towel over her head, and she said it was like being a pudding. I left a bottle of ipecac syrup. Otto would not take my money for the rye loaf he pushed into my arms, and I did not argue, because I had none to spare.

memories.experienced: Grete's shop smelled of camphor and floor polish. She had the big green ledger open on the counter before I got the door shut, as if she had seen me coming down the street. My page was the third from the end. Her neat hand ran down it: a hundred and sixty-six crowns carried from the summer, and the ten I had promised still blank. She said, "You sent me a note in the first week saying the ninth, Ines. It's the ninth."
memories.did: I told her the truth: I could not pay this month, not the ten, not two. The Webers still owed me for the birth, and half the town owed me for something. I asked her to carry it one more month. She wrote 'carried to Nov.' in the margin without a word and underlined it, which was worse than a word. I still bought a bottle of carbolic, on the account, and felt her eyes on my back all the way to the door.

memories.experienced: Anton came back at four as I had told him to. The red streaks had gone back to the wrist and his fever was down; the wound was draining clean. He was easier with me today. While Sanna rewound the bandage he said the gang had drilled a new round at the heading yesterday and Stoll had not looked at a lamp before sending them in. Then he said, "Don't tell Stoll I was here twice. He counts sick days like a miser."
memories.did: I told Anton that I do not discuss patients with foremen, and that if Stoll asks, a burn is a burn. I asked him, lightly, whether the book said point four again yesterday. He grinned and said, "What else would it say?" I gave him a clean sling and told him to come Sunday. After he left I stood at the sink a long time thinking that the contractor makes money by the yard, and a gas reading that never changes costs nobody a yard.

memories.experienced: Father Kurz caught me at the churchyard gate on my way home and walked beside me with his hands in his sleeves. He said the whole parish had noticed my sister wears no ring, and the landlady at the Hart says she pays by the week in coins, not notes, and that the little girl cries at night. He said, very kindly, "A woman does not bring a child up a mountain in October for the air, Doctor."
memories.did: I told him the parish should mind its own confessions. He laughed and said it was his job to mind everyone's. I asked, before I could stop myself, whether Lotte had ever mentioned her husband to him. He said no, only that his name was Friedrich and that she said it the way one says the name of a debt. I said goodnight at my own door and stood in the dark hall for a while before I lit the lamp.

memories.experienced: The tenth came in hard and clear with frost on the inside of the window. The kitchen stove had gone out overnight and the water jug had a skin of ice. Sanna arrived at seven with her nose red and a paper of dripping from her mother. Nobody was waiting yet. The only sound in the clinic was the clock and the cat on the landing.
memories.did: I relit the stove with the last of the kindling and made coffee strong enough to stand a spoon in. I sat at my desk with the casebook and brought the week's cards up to date: Frau Weiss, the carter, the Brandt girl, A. Reis. I ruled a new page for the week. Sanna and I had bread and dripping at the desk. I said, "A quiet morning. I don't trust it," and she told me to stop tempting fate.

memories.experienced: At twenty to twelve a boy from the camp came through the door without knocking, covered in grey dust to the eyebrows, so out of breath he could only point. When he could talk he said, "The roof came down at the face. Four men. Stoll says come now." Up the valley I could hear the camp whistle going in short blasts, the one they use for accidents, over and over.
memories.did: I had the surgical bag packed in three minutes; I keep it half packed for exactly this. I told Sanna to bring the splints, both bottles of chloroform, all the lint we had and the big lamp. We went up the portal road half running, the boy ahead of us, and I made him tell me as we went: who was trapped, who was bleeding, who was talking. He said one was not talking. I stopped asking and ran.

memories.experienced: They had carried the four out of the tunnel mouth and laid them in the mess bunkhouse on trestles. One had his thigh bent where no thigh bends; one a crushed foot; one ribs and a collarbone; one, the quiet one, a scalp laid open and a pupil blown wide on the left. Voss stood by the door in a good coat, very calm. Stoll was shouting at everyone and no one: "The roof was sound! I sounded it myself this morning! Sound as a bell!"
memories.did: I told Stoll to shout outside or hold a lamp, one or the other. I sorted them in order: head first, then the thigh, then the foot, ribs last. I asked Voss for hot water, clean sheets and every lamp in the camp, and he gave the orders at once without arguing, I'll say that for him. I asked the names and wrote them on the men's wrists in pencil: Luka Maric, thigh; Karel Horn, foot; Jiri Benes, ribs; Tomas Kral, head.

memories.experienced: The night went by in lamplight. Kral's skull had a depressed piece the size of a coin; when I lifted it he groaned, and by two in the morning both his pupils were the same size. Maric's femur took three men pulling to set. Anton Reis appeared at some point with his arm in my sling and held the lamp over the table for hours without being asked, steady as a post. Once, with my hands inside the wound, I saw a boy's face that was not there.
memories.did: I trephined Kral with the small crown and cleared the clot. I set Maric's leg and splinted it from armpit to ankle, strapped Benes's ribs, dressed Horn's foot and kept the toes. Around four I told Anton, "Lower. Left. Hold it there," and did not look up for an hour. When the boy's face came I stopped, counted ten breaths the way I taught myself six years ago, and went on cutting. I did not let myself think the name until the sun was up.

memories.experienced: At first light Anton walked me down the camp path because Sanna was staying with Kral. The snow crunched. He said nobody from the office had asked the men what happened, only Stoll, and Stoll was writing it up as a natural fall. Then, without looking at me, he said Stoll had filled in the gas log for that shift at the canteen table the night before, before anyone went near the face. "I saw the pen go. Point four."
memories.did: I asked him straight whether the gas had anything to do with the roof. He said no, the roof was the roof, bad rock and too long between props. "But if he writes the book before the shift, Doctor, what's the book for?" I said I didn't know, and that he should not say it to anyone else yet. I made him show me his hand before we parted at the bridge. It was clean. I told him he had held a good lamp.

memories.experienced: Mayor Dahl was waiting in my front room at nine with his hat on his knee. Maric had been carried down and was in my back room with his leg in the splint. The mayor asked how long before the four men could work, and before I could answer he told me the tunnel is three weeks behind, the company is talking about penalties, and Kessel Pass will be a dead end on the map without it. He said, "We all want the same thing, Doctor."
memories.did: I told him Maric would not walk for three months, Horn would not climb a ladder before Christmas, Benes could lift in six weeks and Kral might be lucky to know his own name. I said I did not want the same thing as a man who counted the tunnel before the men. He said I was tired and stood up. I said I was, and showed him the door, and then I went and sat on the stairs for ten minutes because my legs shook.

memories.experienced: In the afternoon Father Kurz came to sit with Maric, who is Catholic and frightened. On his way out he stopped at my desk and said the old men in the square were talking of nothing but 1891, the year the silver mine came in and took eleven, his predecessor buried them all in one week. He said, "The tunnel runs toward those galleries, you know. The old men say the mountain remembers."
memories.did: I told him mountains do not remember anything, rock is just rock that nobody propped properly. He said that was a very modern thing to say. I asked him, since he knows everything, whether anyone living had been down the old workings. He said a few old men, and that there was a map of them somewhere in the vestry, a drawing from before his time. I said I might like to see it one day. He said it was covered in mouse droppings but I was welcome.

memories.experienced: By evening the house was quiet except for Maric snoring in the back room. The rye loaf from Otto Brandt was on the kitchen table, half gone. My hands smelled of carbolic no matter how often I washed them, and there was blood under two nails. The lamp on my desk was low on oil and ticking as it heated.
memories.did: I wrote up all four men in the casebook while I still remembered the details: Kral, depressed fracture L parietal, trephined 11.40 pm, pupils equal 2 am; Maric, closed fracture R femur; Horn, crush L foot; Benes, fractured ribs 5-7 R and clavicle. At the bottom I wrote 'Foreman states roof sounded that morning'. I ate bread and cold dripping over the page, got crumbs in the binding, and went to bed at eight like an old woman.

memories.experienced: The first proper snow came down in the night and the street was white to the doorsteps. Maric's toes were pink and warm and he had eaten all his porridge. Sanna reported Kral awake at the camp and asking for his mother. The morning clinic was a woman at seven months with swollen ankles, two children with chilblains, and the postman with a boil on his neck that he had been hiding under his scarf for a week.
memories.did: I checked Maric's splint and tightened a strap. I told the pregnant woman to lie on her left side and eat less salt, and wrote her down for Thursday. I rubbed goose fat into the children's heels and told their mother to dry their stockings. I lanced the postman's boil and he fainted clean away onto Sanna, who is small and said something about him I will not write down. We laughed until Maric called through to ask what was funny.

memories.experienced: At noon I went to the station for the crate of dressings the company promised after the collapse. Emil Ott had it in his office by the stove. He said the train was eight minutes late for snow on the line. Then, as he always does, he told me who had been through: a salesman in corsets, two navvies leaving for good, and my sister, who had come down every morning this week to ask if there was post for her. "Every morning, Doctor. And every morning she looks relieved when there isn't."
memories.did: I signed Ott's docket for the crate and asked him if he had ever known anyone relieved to get no letters. He said yes, debtors and wives. I did not like that answer and told him so. He shrugged and helped me load the crate onto a sled. I pulled it back up the street myself, which took twenty minutes and most of my temper, and all the way I kept thinking of Lotte on that platform in the cold, waiting for something she hoped would not come.

memories.experienced: Just after nine that night I was refilling the dispensary lamp with my hands still stupid from the cold. I heard the downstairs bell, turned, and the lamp went off the shelf. Burning oil ran across the floorboards and up into the basket of lint, and the flames were at the bandage shelf before I had moved. Then Lotte was in the doorway with snow on her shoulders, saying my name like she used to when we were girls, "Nessa!"
memories.did: I shouted at her to get back and grabbed for the water jug, which was the wrong thing, oil and water. Lotte did not get back. She tore the rag rug off the floor, threw it over the burning lint and knelt on it, and I pulled the wet blanket off the airing rail and beat the shelf with it until the flames were out. The whole thing lasted perhaps a minute. We were both coughing and black to the wrists. I said, "That was my fault. I was careless." She said, "Yes, you were."

memories.experienced: Afterward we sat on the kitchen floor with our backs to the stove. Lotte had come because Mira had a cough and the Hart's landlady was sitting with her; she meant only to ask for a syrup. She laughed, suddenly, and said, "You set fire to Mother's curtains once, do you remember? You were reading." Then she said, "I am not going back to the city, Ines. Don't ask me why tonight."
memories.did: I made tea and put brandy in both cups. We went through the dispensary together with a candle: lost were all the lint, two rolls of bandage, the bottle of laudanum, and half the labels were scorched off. The quinine tin was blackened but sealed, and I opened it to be sure: the powders were dry. I gave Lotte the cough syrup for Mira and did not ask why. At the door I said, "Thank you, Lotte." She said, "Put the lamp on a lower shelf."

memories.experienced: Sanna came in at seven, smelled the smoke from the hall and walked straight into the dispensary without taking her coat off. She looked at the black streak up the wall and the scorched shelf and said, "Tell me nobody died." When I told her what happened she said a ship's surgeon ought to know better than to fill a lamp while it is lit, and she was right, I had not even turned it down.
memories.did: I let her scold me; I had it coming. We made a list together: forty yards of lint, four rolls of bandage, a new bottle of laudanum, the labels, a new glass for the lamp. Sanna priced it from memory at about eleven crowns. I said the company crate would cover the bandages and the rest would have to go on Grete's book, and saw Sanna's face when I said it. I told her, "Yes, I know," before she could.

memories.experienced: I went down to the market at eleven for potatoes and onions. The snow had turned to slush and the stalls were half empty. Coming back I took the short way by Mill Lane without thinking, and the old surgery was there as it always is: shutters nailed, the four screw holes where my brass plate hung, a drift of snow against the step where the Anko woman sat all that night six years ago.
memories.did: I bought four pounds of potatoes and a string of onions and argued the onion woman down by a heller. On Mill Lane I kept my eyes on the far end of the street and walked at an even pace past the old clinic and did not look at the door. I counted my steps to the corner, forty-two. I told myself it was only a building. At home I peeled the potatoes much harder than potatoes need.

memories.experienced: In the afternoon I took Lotte's scarf back to the Hart; she had left it on my kitchen chair. She was alone in their room at the window with a sheet of paper, closely written in a man's slanting hand, the envelope beside her. When the door opened she folded the letter in two quick movements, pushed it under the lining of her sewing basket and put the basket on the floor behind her skirt.
memories.did: I pretended I had not seen it. I put the scarf on the bed and said, "You left this, and the rug you ruined was a very ugly rug." She smiled, not quite. I asked how Mira's cough was and she said better. I did not ask about the letter, though the question was in my mouth the whole ten minutes I was there. On the stairs I understood that Ott was wrong: something had come for her after all.

memories.experienced: Teodor Lind had sent a note asking me to look at the school heads for lice, since two children were scratching. The schoolhouse was warm, twenty-two children on benches, a stove glowing red. Teodor stood at the back with his sleeves rolled up and chalk on his cheek. Mira sat in the second row. She saw me come in and put her head down over her slate and kept it down the whole time.
memories.did: I went along the benches with my comb and my lamp and found lice on three of them, none on Mira, which I told Teodor quietly so the others would not hear. When I got to Mira I only said, "Clean as a whistle," and moved on without touching her hair. I wrote out a note for the three families about vinegar and fine combs. Teodor said the children would remember me as the comb woman. I said I had been called worse.

memories.experienced: Teodor locked the schoolhouse and said he was going my way, which he is not; he lodges at the other end of town. It was dark by five. We walked through the slush while he talked about the children, and asked about the men from the collapse, and said the whole school had heard the whistle and he had kept them singing so they would not be frightened. At my door he said, "You look as though you haven't slept in a week."
memories.did: I told him about Kral's skull and the coin-sized piece, and he did not flinch, which I liked. I said the singing was clever. When he said I looked tired I said I had set my own dispensary on fire, and he laughed so hard he had to lean on the lamp post. At the door I said goodnight twice because I forgot I had already said it. I stood inside with my back to the door and told myself not to be a fool at thirty-eight.

memories.experienced: Sunday. I slept until seven, which has not happened in a month. The church bells went at nine and I did not go. Outside the snow was melting off the roofs in long drips. Sanna had the day off. At ten a man brought his little boy with an earache, the eardrum red and bulging, the child screaming with it. Maric had his breakfast and asked if I had a deck of cards.
memories.did: I warmed a few drops of oil and put them in the boy's ear, gave him a paper of aspirin powder cut small, and told the father to come back if the ear began to run. I found Maric my father's old deck with the queen of hearts missing and we played piquet for matches while the sheets boiled in the copper. He beat me four games to one and said doctors cannot count.

memories.experienced: Anton came at eleven for his last dressing. The palm had closed into a shiny pink scar and he could make a fist again, slowly. He said he was back on the powder tomorrow. Then he saw my casebook open on the desk and asked what I had written about him. He said, "Not what I said about the book, Doctor. Stoll can read."
memories.did: I told him my case notes are for me, in my own hand, and that Stoll does not come in this house. But I turned back to his page, and while he watched I scratched out 'readings same every shift - 0.4' so thoroughly the pen went through the paper. When he had gone I wrote it again on the back flyleaf in the ship's shorthand I learned at sea, which nobody in Kessel Pass can read, with the date and the words 'per A.R., written before the shift'.

memories.experienced: Konrad Voss came himself at one with an envelope. He admired the new snow and asked after Kral. Then he laid out thirty crowns in notes on my desk for the four men and said the company would pay for Maric and Kral in full, but Horn and Benes had signed off the shift ten minutes before the fall and were strictly on their own time. When I asked him about the gas readings at the heading, he smiled and said, "The gas is quite safe, Doctor. Stoll keeps an excellent log."
memories.did: I told him I had billed forty-six, not thirty, and that ten minutes did not make a man's ribs less broken. He said the matter was closed and buttoned his coat. I took the thirty because I needed it. After he left I counted it twice and did the sum: eleven for the fire, ten for Grete this month, coal, the Hart. It did not reach. I put eight aside for the dispensary and none for Grete, and hated myself for it.

memories.experienced: At four Teodor knocked with a sheet of drawing paper rolled under his arm. He said the children had drawn 'a house in our town' and he thought I should see one of them. It was Mira's. A tall grey house with a red door, and a sign over it with a cross, and at the top window a woman with her hair in a knot, holding a lamp. Underneath, in careful capitals: THE DOCTORS HOUSE.
memories.did: I held it for a long time and could not think of a thing to say. Teodor said, "She asked me how to spell doctor." I said the door is actually green, and he said he would not tell her. I asked if I could keep it, and he said Mira had said nothing either way, which from Mira was permission. I pinned it above my desk with two tacks, next to the anatomical chart, and gave Teodor coffee, and we both looked at it instead of at each other.

memories.experienced: Supper at the Hart again. Mira's cough was nearly gone. She sat by the window watching the sparrows on the stable roof while the landlady brought dumplings. Lotte looked less grey than last week. She said the inn was the kind of place Mother would have called 'honest', which was Mother's worst word, and for a second we were both back in that lawyer's office with the brooch on the table between us.
memories.did: I did not pick up the thread about Mother; I let it lie. I told Mira I had seen a drawing of a house with a red door, and that it was hanging over my desk now. She did not look at me, but she stopped watching the sparrows and ate her dumpling. I told Lotte about the thirty crowns and made a joke of it. Walking home I thought the brooch was probably in Lotte's case, and that I did not care as much as I had for nine years.

memories.experienced: Sanna had the stove lit by seven and the waiting bench already full: a navvy with a wrist the size of a turnip, the carter's wife with her usual heartburn, and a boy who had swallowed a button and was very proud of it. The wrist was sprained, not broken; I felt the bones twice to be sure. While she rolled bandages Sanna told me a man in a long grey coat had got off the evening train and stood on the platform writing in a little book, 'like he was counting the snow.'
memories.did: I strapped the navvy's wrist in a figure-of-eight and told him no shovel for five days, which he heard as two. I gave the carter's wife bicarbonate and the same lecture about pickled herring. I told the button boy's mother to watch the chamber pot, and she looked at me as if I had said something obscene. Then I wrote all three into my casebook, dated the fifteenth, and asked Sanna, 'Grey coat. Railway or insurance?' She said, 'He had good boots.' I said that narrowed it to anyone not from here.

memories.experienced: The crate of carbolic and lint I had ordered was sitting on the platform under a tarpaulin, and Emil Ott came out of his office wiping his spectacles. He said the man in the grey coat had come up on yesterday evening's train with a railway pass, not a ticket, and had asked him how many workmen's coffins had gone down the line since spring. The man himself was at the far end of the platform, bareheaded in the cold, looking up at the ridge where the portal is. He did not look at me.
memories.did: I signed Ott's docket for the crate and asked what he had told the man. Ott said, 'The truth. Two. And a finger in a matchbox, which I don't count.' I said the finger was mine, I had sent it down to the family for burial because they asked. I looked at the grey coat a while longer than was polite, then got the porter's boy to wheel the crate to the clinic for four hellers. On the way I found myself counting the coffins myself, and got three, not two, because Ott had forgotten the winter.

memories.experienced: Otto Brandt's shop smelled of caraway and wet wool. He wrapped my rye loaf and then, instead of handing it over, asked if I would 'just listen' to Mila, who was sitting on a flour sack behind the counter in two cardigans, doing sums on a slate. Her breathing was quick but not labouring. Through the stethoscope there was a fine wheeze on the left base, no worse than last week. She told me seven times eight was fifty-four and was insulted when I disagreed.
memories.did: I knelt on the floury boards and listened to both sides of her back, front and back again. I told Otto the chest was no worse, to keep her out of the ovens' steam and away from the cold yard, and to send for me if her lips went blue or she could not finish a sentence. I told Mila that seven eights were fifty-six and that I would bet her a bun on it. She checked on her fingers, lost, and Otto gave me the bun anyway and would not take money for the loaf.

memories.experienced: At the Hart the fire in the back parlour was smoking. Lotte was mending a stocking and said 'Ines' the way you say the name of a street. Mira sat at the far end of the table with her drawing book and did not lift her head once in forty minutes. She was drawing birds, rows of them, each on a line like washing. When I put a tin of barley sugar near her elbow she moved her elbow away. Lotte's hands were busy the whole time; she never let them rest in her lap.
memories.did: I asked Lotte whether the room was warm enough and whether the landlady was overcharging her for coal. She said 'It's fine' to both. I said the barley sugar was for anyone who wanted it and left it on the table. To Mira I said only, 'That one's a wagtail,' pointing at a bird with a long tail, and got nothing. I did not ask Lotte why she had come, though it sat in my mouth like a stone. I left at half past eight and on the stairs I noticed I had been holding my shoulders up round my ears.

memories.experienced: The dressing round at the camp took the morning: Kral's scalp healing clean over the trephine hole, Benes's ribs knitting, Horn's crushed foot still weeping; Maric had gone down the line to the valley hospital on yesterday's train, splint and all. Walking back past the portal I saw the man in the grey coat standing with Jakob Stoll by the lamp cabin. Stoll had his arms folded and was talking loudly about 'every shift, by the book'. The stranger said something too quiet to hear and wrote it down. Stoll saw me, stopped mid-word, and turned his back so that the stranger had to turn too.
memories.did: I finished rebandaging Horn's foot first, because that was the job, and told him to keep it up on a crate. Then I took the long way past the lamp cabin, which is not the long way at all, and said, 'Morning, Stoll.' He said, 'Doctor,' and nothing else. I nodded to the man in grey; he raised his hat an inch. I wrote in my casebook that evening that three of the four collapse men were mending, and under it, for no medical reason, 'Stoll nervous.'

memories.experienced: Anton Reis came in at two for what should have been the last look at his hand. The burn had closed; new skin, pink and shiny across the palm, the fingers stiff but working. He would not sit still. He asked twice whether anyone had been asking about him. Then he said, not looking at me, that a man in a grey coat had asked the shot-firers how often the lamps were checked, and that nobody had answered because Stoll was standing right there.
memories.did: I made him grip my two fingers and squeeze until I said stop, and wrote 'grip good, ROM 80 per cent' in the casebook. I told him to rub lanolin into the scar twice a day or it would crack in the cold. When he mentioned the lamps I asked, 'And how often are they checked?' He said, 'Every shift. Same as the readings. Same as everything.' I asked what he meant by that and he said, 'Nothing, Doctor,' and paid me in coins that were still warm from his pocket.

memories.experienced: Grete's shop bell is louder than it needs to be. She had my carbolic ready on the counter and her ledger open beside it before I had my gloves off, the ribbon marker already at my page. She said, not unkindly, that the wholesaler in the valley had put up the price of quinine by a fifth and that her own next delivery would be late because of snow on the lower line. The stove behind her was ticking. A woman I did not know was waiting behind me and pretending not to listen.
memories.did: I asked for two bottles of carbolic and one of laudanum and said, 'On the account, Grete,' in the voice I use for bad news to patients. She wrote it in, in her small upright hand, and turned the book so I could initial the line. I initialled it. I said I would pay something at the end of the month, and she said, 'You said that at the end of the last one,' and then, 'I'm not dunning you, Ines, I'm telling you the price of quinine.' I said thank you and meant both halves of it.

memories.experienced: Teodor was still at the schoolhouse at five, sweeping chalk dust into a pan with the stove going out. He showed me Mira's copybook without my asking: her letters were careful and small, and every margin had a bird in it. He said she had asked him that morning whether birds had bones like people. He said he had told her yes, hollow ones, and that she had written 'hollow' three times to get the spelling. He smelled of chalk and pipe tobacco and he laughed at his own jokes before he finished them.
memories.did: I turned the pages of the copybook slowly and said, 'She doesn't talk to me at all.' He said, 'She doesn't talk to anyone for the first month. She's listening.' I said I hoped she was hearing something useful. He walked me back as far as the pump on Kirchgasse, which is not on his way, and I let him. At the pump I said, 'Goodnight, Teo,' and noticed I had used the short name. He noticed too. I went upstairs and did not light the lamp for a while.

memories.experienced: At half past eight the man in the grey coat walked into the surgery, took off his hat, and said, 'Dr. Calder. My name is Hale. Inspector, Railway Safety Board.' He had a flat northern accent and chilblains on his knuckles. He said he had read the contractor's report on the fall at the face and that it was two paragraphs long. He asked how long I had been doctor here and whether I treated the tunnel men. He did not ask anything else, which I liked, and said he would come back when he knew what to ask.
memories.did: I said, 'Six years, and yes, all of them I can get my hands on.' I told him I keep a casebook of every patient, and that he could not read it, but I could answer questions from it if he had a right to ask them. He said that was fair. I told Sanna to give him the chair nearest the stove, because his hands were purple, and he took it. When he left I wrote 'Hale, Inspector, R.S.B.' on the back page of the casebook and underlined it.

memories.experienced: More snow came down off the ridge at noon, fat and wet, and the clinic went quiet the way it always does when people decide their coughs can wait. Sanna and I had the lint and bandages out of the new crate and on the counting table. She counted aloud in threes, which she learned from her grandmother, and I lost count twice listening to her. The soup she had brought in a can was cabbage and potato and needed salt.
memories.did: I counted forty-two rolls of bandage and nineteen packets of lint, and Sanna counted forty-one and nineteen, so we counted again and got forty-two. I shelved them on the good side of the dispensary, away from the scorched boards. I salted the soup, ate it standing up, and told Sanna to go home before the lane filled in. She said, 'And who answers the bell?' I said I would, since that is roughly my entire profession. She went at two.

memories.experienced: Father Kurz caught me on the church steps and told me, before I had asked anything, that the inspector was lodging at the Hart, took his eggs soft, and had asked him about the old workings. That was why I went in. In the vestry he unlocked a flat oak press and took out a roll of linen-backed paper, brown at the edges, tied with tape. He said it was the survey of the silver mine drawn in 1884, left to the parish by the last mine captain, and that no one had asked for it in years.
memories.did: I asked if I could borrow it. He said, 'For a doctor, anything, for the mayor, over my dead body,' and laughed, and then made me write my name and the date in the parish day-book so he could say where it had gone. I wrote 'Map of the silver mine, borrowed 17th, I. Calder.' I carried it home under my coat against the snow and told him I would bring it back within the week. I did not tell him why I wanted it, because I did not quite know.

memories.experienced: On the kitchen table upstairs the map was bigger than I expected: five galleries fanning out from a main shaft, the levels marked in fathoms, a compass rose in faded red. Gallery Four was hatched over in a later ink, with a note in a different hand: 'Fall of 14 March 1891. Eleven men.' Eleven names were written in a column beside it. The ridge contour and the lower end of Gallery Two ran closer to the line the railway surveyors had pegged than I had imagined.
memories.did: I weighed the corners down with the teapot, the lamp, my casebook and a boot. I found the pegged tunnel line by guessing from the church and the portal, and drew it very lightly in pencil on a sheet of tracing paper laid over the map, not on the map itself. I read the eleven names aloud to myself, which was stupid, and recognised two surnames from the churchyard. I sat until the lamp guttered wondering whether anyone at the contractor's office had ever seen this sheet.

memories.experienced: At ten to eleven someone knocked on the back door, not the bell. It was Anton Reis with a sack under his arm and snow on his shoulders. In the kitchen he took out a brass safety lamp and turned it so the light caught the gauze. The seam at the top of the gauze cylinder had been opened and crimped shut again; the crimp was uneven and there was a gap I could get a fingernail into. He said, 'It won't show gas like that. The flame won't cap. It'll just burn.'
memories.did: I asked where he got it. He said it was the lamp Stoll's cabin had issued him that week, and that when he took it back and asked for another he was told they were all checked. I asked who else knew. He said, 'You.' I said, 'Why me, not the inspector?' and he said the inspector goes home and he does not. I told him I would keep it, locked, and tell no one his name. I wrapped it back in the sack and put it in the dispensary press and gave him a glass of plum brandy before he went.

memories.experienced: In daylight the lamp looked worse. Under my hand lens the gauze was cut along the seam for nearly two inches and pressed shut with pliers; I could see the teeth marks on the brass. The lamp was stamped 'No. 27' on the base. It smelled of paraffin and of the tunnel, that wet-stone smell. The dispensary shelf it sat on still had a black tongue on it from my own fire last week, which I did not enjoy being reminded of.
memories.did: I drew the seam and the pliers marks in my casebook, full size, with the number 27, and wrote 'given me 17th, 10.50 p.m., by a shot-firer' without his name. I locked the lamp in the press and put the key on the string round my neck with the dispensary key. I thought about walking to the Hart and showing Hale, and decided I would not until I knew more; a lamp in a doctor's cupboard proves only that a doctor has a lamp. Then Sanna came in and I put the lens away.

memories.experienced: A boy from the camp came running at eleven, red-faced, to say two men in bunkhouse two were 'burning up and shitting blood'. It was not blood, it turned out, but it was bad enough. Jonas Mraz, nineteen, had a temperature of 104 and a belly so tender he screamed when I pressed below the ribs. Bela Horvat, older, was 103 and talking to his mother, who is in Szeged. The bunkhouse stank. Both had been well on Sunday.
memories.did: I had them moved to the two bunks nearest the door, where the air was least bad, and gave each a quinine powder in water and a spoonful of laudanum for the gut. I asked what they had eaten and drunk since Sunday; the answer was the same stew and bread as everybody, and water from the camp barrels. I wrote their names, ages, temperatures and the time, 11.40, on a page I headed 'Camp fever' and then crossed 'fever' out and wrote 'illness', because I did not know yet.

memories.experienced: Jakob Stoll found me in the doorway of bunkhouse two and wanted to know when Mraz and Horvat would be back on shift, because he was two men short on the heading already after the fall. He said the Herr Chief Engineer did not pay men to lie in bed. He stood with his boots apart and would not come inside; I think he was afraid of catching it. Behind him a queue of men for the noon meal were watching us.
memories.did: I said, 'When their temperature is normal for two days. Not before.' He said Voss would want them back Monday. I said Voss could come and take their temperatures himself and I would lend him the thermometer. Then I said, loudly enough for the queue, that anyone with a headache and a hot belly was to come to me, not work it off, and that I would not charge them. Stoll said, 'You'll bankrupt yourself.' I said that was my business, and it is, unfortunately.

memories.experienced: Back at the clinic Sanna had kept the evening surgery going: a sore throat, a drunk with a cut lip, nothing I needed to see. She had also, without being asked, counted the fever powders. There were thirty-eight quinine powders left in the drawer and one large bottle of tincture. She said, 'Two men, three powders a day each,' and let me do the rest. The lamp over the counting table flickered because I had trimmed it badly again.
memories.did: Thirty-eight powders at six a day is six days, and that if nobody else took sick. I wrote to the valley wholesaler direct for two hundred powders, not through Grete, asking for terms, and then tore it up and wrote it again asking for a hundred, because I knew what two hundred would cost. I entered both camp men in the casebook with the day's temperatures. I told Sanna, 'If three more come in, we are in trouble,' and she said, 'Then we'll be in trouble,' and put her coat on.

memories.experienced: I could not sleep. The fever men's names kept going round, and under them, the way it always does when I am frightened, the other name. From the kitchen window, if I lean, I can see the corner of Mill Lane and the roof of the old surgery with the snow sliding off it. I remembered, clearly and for no useful reason, the exact weight of the lamp I held for myself that night because the orderly had gone for more chloroform, and the Anko boy's small hand going slack on the sheet.
memories.did: I got up and made tea I did not drink. I told myself out loud that two fevers in a camp are two fevers in a camp, and that I had seen it coming no more than anyone could. I did not believe myself. I did not take out the old casebook; I have not opened that year in six years and I was not going to start at two in the morning. I stood at the window until my feet were numb, looking at the roof on Mill Lane and not going there, and then I went back to bed.

memories.experienced: I was cutting behind the Hart to the camp road at a quarter to eight when I found Mira crouched by the woodpile in her school coat. She had a hen sparrow cupped in her mitten; its left wing hung down and dragged. She looked up at me and said, in a clear small voice, the first words she has ever said to me: 'It fell off the roof. Can you fix it? You fix people.' Her nose was running and she did not care.
memories.did: I said, 'Let's see,' and squatted beside her. The wing was not broken at the shoulder, only at the wrist joint, I thought. I folded it against the body and bound it with a strip of lint from my bag, round and round, not too tight, leaving the good wing and legs free. I told her it must live in a box with holes and eat crumbs and not try to fly for three weeks. She said, 'Three weeks,' very seriously. I walked her to the schoolhouse with the sparrow in my hat and handed both to Teodor at the door.

memories.experienced: The camp had four now. Two new since yesterday in bunkhouse four and bunkhouse one, the same pattern: fever over 103, gut pain, headache behind the eyes, one with a pink spotty rash on the belly I did not like the look of. Mraz was worse; Horvat a shade better. The inspector was standing at the edge of the path by the drying shed, and when I came out he asked, very quietly, how many. The camp barrels by the cookhouse had a skin of ice on them.
memories.did: I told Hale, 'Four. By the end of the week I'd guess eight,' and then wished I had not guessed out loud. I gave out six quinine powders and wrote down each man's water barrel, bunk and what he had eaten, pages of it, looking for one thing they all shared and finding only that they all lived in a tunnel camp. I broke the ice on the cookhouse barrel and smelled it; it smelled of nothing but cold. I asked the cook to boil all drinking water. He said he would, in a voice that meant he would not.

memories.experienced: The afternoon was a tooth. Frau Pichler, who keeps the post office, had had a back molar aching for a month and had decided today was the day, because it was Friday and she does unpleasant things on Fridays. The tooth was cracked to the root and came out in two pieces. She held onto the arm of the chair so hard that she cracked the varnish. Afterwards she paid me in a dozen eggs and a stamped envelope, which she said she always had spare.
memories.did: I gave her a pledget of cotton soaked in clove oil to bite on and told her no hot drinks until tomorrow and nothing chewy for a week. She asked if she could keep the tooth; I washed both halves and gave them to her in a twist of paper. I put the eggs in the cold pantry and the envelope in the drawer, where it will sit until I have someone to write to. Then I wiped down the chair and noticed the varnish, and decided it was a better record of the extraction than anything I would write.

memories.experienced: I told Lotte, in the parlour at the Hart, that Mira had spoken to me. Her face did something complicated and then she smiled properly, the first time I have seen that smile in nine years. Then she reached across for the teapot and her sleeve rode up: on the inside of her forearm there were four bruises in a row, going yellow at the edges, the size of fingertips. She pulled the sleeve down at once and said, 'I fell on the ice by the station. Clumsy.' Mira was already asleep upstairs.
memories.did: I said, 'Falling doesn't do that, Lotte. Falling does the heel of the hand and the elbow.' She said, 'Well, I did it differently,' and poured the tea and talked about the sparrow for ten minutes without stopping. I let her. I thought of the letter she had shoved under the mending the week before and of the husband I know only as a name, Friedrich, and I did not say either. I left two arnica pads on the table and said, 'For the fall.' She did not look at them.

memories.experienced: At the camp there were five: another in bunkhouse two, a cook's boy of sixteen. Anton Reis was waiting by the drying shed when I came out, not sick, but grey around the eyes. He asked in a low voice whether 'the thing' was safe. He said the lamp cabin had been reorganised on Thursday, new numbers painted on the shelves, and that when he went for his lamp the clerk had looked at him for a long time. He said, 'Maybe it's nothing.' He said it twice.
memories.did: I told him the lamp was locked away where no one would find it without taking my neck off first. I asked whether any of the other shot-firers had lamps like it; he said he had not dared look. I told him to eat, to drink only boiled water because of the fever, and to come to the clinic if he wanted to talk rather than meeting me by a shed where the whole camp can see. He said, 'The whole camp sees the clinic too, Doctor.' I gave the cook's boy his quinine and wrote five names in the book.

memories.experienced: Saturday market in the square was half its size because of the snow. I bought a sack of potatoes, a piece of streaky bacon and a jar of plum jam from the Unterberger woman, who asked after my sister before she asked what I wanted. Across the square, by the fountain that doesn't run in winter, Marta Anko was buying onions. She saw me. She finished paying, picked up her basket, and walked away down the side street without hurrying, the way she has done for six years.
memories.did: I paid for the jam and said my sister was well, which is a lie I tell more easily every week. I did not cross the square. I stood there with the potatoes cutting into my fingers and counted to twenty, which is what I do, and then I walked home the long way so I would not have to go down the same side street. I wanted very badly to have something to say to her and I had nothing new. The boy is dead, and I held the knife.

memories.experienced: Grete had the quinine: one tin of fifty powders that had come up on that morning's goods train after all. She put it on the counter and kept her hand on the lid. She said she had heard about the camp from the carter and that the price had gone up again, to eleven hellers a powder. She opened the ledger to my page. The column was long. She said, 'I'll give you this one on the account. After this I need something paid, Ines. I have a wholesaler too.'
memories.did: I said, 'I know. I'll bring something on the first,' and I meant it, and I did the sum in my head and did not like it. I initialled the line, 'Quinine 50, on acct.', and wrote the date myself because my hand was steadier than hers by then. I told her there were five cases at the camp and that I thought there would be more. She said, 'Then God help your account,' and gave me a paper of peppermints for nothing. I carried the tin home inside my coat like a baby.

memories.experienced: Teodor knocked at seven with a shoebox under his arm. The sparrow was in it, on a bed of torn newspaper, bound wing and all, pecking at a crust. He said Mira had insisted it could not spend the night at the Hart because the landlady's cat was 'looking at it', and had sent it to me, 'because she's the doctor.' He had brought half a cheese and a bottle of wine from the valley that he said was terrible. It was.
memories.did: I put the box by the stove, not too near, and checked the binding; it had held, and the bird bit me, which I took as a good sign. We ate bread and cheese at the kitchen table with the mine map rolled up at one end to make room. He asked what it was and I said, 'Homework.' We drank the terrible wine and he told me about his first school, in a village where the goats came into lessons. He left at a quarter past nine. I sat looking at the shoebox for a long time.

memories.experienced: Hale came to the clinic at eight, before surgery, and stood with his hat in his hands. He said he had heard there were fever cases at the camp and asked the number. He said the contractor's office had told him there were 'a few colds'. He asked, carefully, whether I thought it was connected with the work in the tunnel. He looked around the surgery while he talked, the way a man does who is trained to look, and his eyes rested for a second on the locked dispensary press.
memories.did: I said, 'Five as of yesterday, and none of them has a cold.' I said I did not know the cause and would not pretend to. He asked if there was anything else he ought to know about the tunnel. I thought about the lamp behind that door and the key against my breastbone and said, 'Not yet.' He said 'Not yet' was an honest answer and he would take it. After he left I sat down on the patient's chair and was annoyed with myself for five minutes and then was not.

memories.experienced: Six at the camp now: a navvy called Ferenc, raving, fighting the blanket. Mraz's fever had broken in the night and he asked for soup. I sat with the list of the six and it did not add up to anything: three bunkhouses, two gangs, different shifts, one cook's boy. Konrad Voss came down from the site office in a good fur collar while I was at Ferenc's bunk. He stood in the doorway, not quite in, and said he trusted I would not alarm the men. He said, 'Illness is bad for morale, Doctor. So is talk.'
