memories.did: I gave Ferenc laudanum and two powders and had two men hold him while I sponged him down. I told Voss, 'I don't alarm men. Fevers do.' I asked him where the camp drinking water came from and he said, 'From the ground, like everyone's,' and smiled. I thought of lamp No. 27 in my cupboard and kept my face still. I said the men needed boiled water and a proper sick hut and he said he would 'consider it'. I wrote down six names, six bunks, six temperatures, and underlined none of them because nothing stood out.

memories.experienced: The afternoon was ordinary and I was grateful. The blacksmith's boy had a splinter of iron in the ball of his thumb; old Herr Zauner came in for his ears to be syringed and told me the same story about the Emperor's visit in 1868 that he tells every time; a young mother wanted to know whether her baby's hiccups were dangerous. They were not. Sanna, who had come in though it was Sunday, made coffee strong enough to stand a spoon in and the snow outside turned blue as it got dark.
memories.did: I got the splinter out with a needle and a magnet and gave the boy the splinter to keep, which cheered him more than the sweet. I syringed Herr Zauner's ears, brought out a plug of wax like a cork, and let him finish the story about the Emperor. I told the young mother, 'Hiccups are a baby practising breathing. Feed her and wait.' I sent Sanna home at five and locked the front door at half past, and for once I did not write anything in the casebook I would have to worry about later.

memories.experienced: With the lamp lit and the sparrow asleep in its shoebox, I unrolled the mine map again beside my casebook. By the pencil line on my tracing, the tunnel heading runs toward the end of Gallery Two, and the hatched square of Gallery Four is only a little further on. Eleven dead in 1891. Four hurt at the face eleven days ago. Six in the fever beds tonight. None of these numbers had anything to do with each other, as far as I could tell, and I did not like how they sat on the same table.
memories.did: I wrote a list in the back of the casebook: 'Fall at face, 10th. Lamp 27, gauze opened. Six fevers, no pattern. Gallery Two - how near?' I wrote to the county surveyor's office asking whether the contractor had filed a copy of the 1884 mine survey, and sealed it with Frau Pichler's stamped envelope. I rolled the map up and tied the tape, meaning to return it to Father Kurz by Tuesday, and then untied it again and left it out. I went to bed at midnight without deciding anything.

memories.experienced: The camp was grey at six, frost on the bunkhouse steps. Seven men with the fever now, up from six last night: all the same, heat you could feel through the blanket, cramping low in the belly, tongues coated white. A big Tyrolean in bunkhouse two had vomited twice in the night and his mate had just covered it with sawdust. The quinine tin in my bag rattled more than it should. Someone had nailed a horseshoe over the door of bunkhouse five, which was about as much public health as the company had managed.
memories.did: I went bed to bed and took temperatures, the worst 40.2. I gave three grains of quinine each to the four hottest and told the others water, boiled, as much as they could hold down. I asked every man what he had eaten and drunk since Thursday and wrote it all in the casebook in a column, because I had no idea which answer mattered. Then I counted the tin: twenty-six powders left. I said to nobody in particular, 'Well, that won't last the week,' and went home to open the clinic.

memories.experienced: Back at the clinic Sanna had the stove going and the kettle on and a queue of two. Frau Wendt, the carter's wife, had fallen on the ice by the pump and held her right wrist against her chest like a kitten. It was swollen over the thumb side but the bones moved clean. Behind her a farm boy had a fish hook through the ball of his thumb and was very proud of it. Sanna told me I had frost in my eyebrows.
memories.did: I strapped Frau Wendt's wrist in a figure-of-eight bandage and told her no washing for a week, which she said was the best news she had had since her wedding. I pushed the hook through and snipped the barb with the wire cutters, and gave the boy the hook back in a twist of paper because he asked. Between the two I drank Sanna's coffee standing up and ate half a heel of rye. I told Sanna we would need the big pan for boiling cloths from now on.

memories.experienced: Grete Ammer stood behind her counter with the ledger already open, as if she had seen me crossing the square. She ran her finger down my page without looking at me: a hundred and eighty-seven crowns and sixty owing, nothing paid since the twenty I brought her at the start of the month. She said, quite kindly, which was worse, 'Ines, I can't. Not another powder on the book. I have a supplier in the city who does not care that you are a good woman.' The shop smelled of camphor and floor wax.
memories.did: I asked for two ounces of quinine sulphate on account. When she said no I did not argue, and I did not tell her why I needed it, because I would not beg in front of the Hofer woman buying corn plasters. I paid cash for one bottle of laudanum, which left me with four crowns in my purse, and said, 'Put the rest where you like, Grete.' Outside I stood on the step and did the sum again in my head. Seven men and twenty-six powders.

memories.experienced: Supper at the Hart with Lotte and Mira: mutton stew, too much salt, a table by the stove. Mira ate with her elbows tucked in and her eyes on me, and halfway through she asked whether the bird with the broken wing would be able to fly by spring. Lotte laughed at something the innkeeper said and then pulled her cuff down over her wrist without seeming to notice she did it. The yellow on her forearm had not quite gone.
memories.did: I told Mira the truth: some birds fly again and some learn to live on the ground, and that a strip of lint was the best I could do for a sparrow. She said Herr Lind had said it could live in its box by the school stove, where the whole class could feed it. I said I would carry it over in the morning if she let me come and look at it there. She nodded, once, which I counted. I did not ask Lotte about the wrist. I paid for my own stew with one of my four crowns and walked home.

memories.experienced: Emil Ott caught me on the platform when I went to collect a crate of bandage lint off the 8.10. He held out an envelope with a city postmark and a printed crest, and said, 'Official, Doctor. I didn't open it,' in a voice that meant he wished he had. It was from the Municipal Hospital. They offered me the post of assistant surgeon, two hundred and eighty crowns a month and rooms, to begin in the spring, and asked for an answer within six weeks.
memories.did: I read it twice standing in the wind, then folded it into my coat pocket so Ott could not read my face. I signed for the lint and for the postcard that came with it, the valley wholesaler regretting that he could not send quinine to a new customer on credit, and told him, 'It's a bill, Emil,' which he did not believe. On the walk back I worked out that two hundred and eighty crowns would clear Grete's hundred and eighty-seven in a single month. I did not tell Sanna. I put the letter under the blotter on my desk and started morning surgery.

memories.experienced: At the camp there were nine now. The worst was a navvy called Pavel Hruby, nineteen, from somewhere past Brno, who had been at work on Monday and was now grey and talking to his mother in Czech. His pulse was thin and fast, a hundred and thirty, and his belly was tight as a drum. The men had put his boots under his bunk side by side, very neatly, which I did not like at all.
memories.did: I gave Pavel four grains of quinine and got half a pint of boiled water with salt and sugar into him a spoon at a time. I told his bunkmate, a quiet Slovak named Juraj, to keep him on his side and fetch me at the clinic if he stopped answering. I wrote Pavel's name at the top of a fresh casebook page and underlined it. Walking down I kept asking myself what nine men had in common that the other hundred did not.

memories.experienced: Grete came in the back door at four with her shawl over her head and a parcel under her arm. Father Kurz had been in the shop, she said, and told her there were nine men down at the camp and one of them dying. 'You might have said,' she told me. The parcel was an ounce of quinine sulphate and a box of Dover's powders. She had written it into the ledger already; she showed me the line.
memories.did: I told her I had not said because I did not want it to sound like a trick. She said it sounded like pride, and she was right. I thanked her properly, both hands. We agreed I would pay two crowns a week off the old account and the fever stock would go on a separate page 'till it's over'. Sanna weighed the powders out into papers while we talked. When Grete left I sat down for a minute on the dispensary stool.

memories.experienced: Late, the house quiet, the stove ticking as it cooled. The hospital letter was still under the blotter and I could see the corner of the crest. Somewhere up the valley a train whistled for the tunnel curve. My hand ached from writing, and my feet had gone numb in the draught under the desk. Nine names on the fever pages, and the ink on the last one still wet. The clinic clock said ten past one when I finally looked at it.
memories.did: I brought the casebook up to date by lamplight: nine fever cases, each with age, bunkhouse, day of onset, temperature, what they drank, what they ate. Then I took out the letter and read it again and tried to imagine a ward with gas lighting and a porter to carry things. I wrote 'assistant surgeon' on a scrap and looked at it and burned the scrap in the stove. I did not decide anything. I went to bed at half past one.

memories.experienced: Juraj knocked at twenty past three and I went up with him in the dark. Pavel did not know me. He was burning, and then around half past four the heat seemed to go out of him all at once and his breathing went long and far apart. He died at twenty to five. Stoll came in with a lantern a few minutes after and looked at the bunk and said, 'He was never strong, that one.' Pavel weighed perhaps nine stone.
memories.did: I closed his eyes and wrote the time on my cuff because I had no paper. I told Stoll he had been strong enough to carry rail on Monday. Stoll said the company would see to the burial. I said I would see to the certificate, and I did, at the bunkhouse table: typhoid-like fever, cause undetermined. I told Juraj to burn the straw from the mattress and wash his own hands in hot water until they hurt.

memories.experienced: Father Kurz met me at the lychgate of St. Veit's. He already knew about Pavel; he always knows. He said the company had asked for the plot at the bottom by the wall, the cheap one, and that Mayor Dahl had asked him to 'keep the service short, for morale'. Then, in his other voice, he asked whether I was finished with the mine map from the vestry, as the bishop's man was coming in December to count things.
memories.did: I told him to give the boy the plot under the yew and send the difference in the bill to Voss. He said he would do it and argue later. I said the map was on my table and I had not finished with it, that I kept looking at the galleries under the ridge and the date of the old fall. He said, 'Keep it till Advent, then.' I sat in the back pew for ten minutes before I went down to open surgery.

memories.experienced: The two o'clock from the city brought a man in a camel coat with a leather bag and a folding rubber bath, which was how I knew what he was before Ott said it. Voss was on the platform to meet him, hat in hand, which I had never seen. Ott leaned over to me and said, 'The company's own doctor. Brenner. They wired for him Monday.' Brenner looked at the ridge and said the air was very bracing.
memories.did: I went over and introduced myself. Brenner shook my hand, called me 'Fraulein Doktor Calder', and said he had heard I had been 'holding the fort'. I told him there were nine cases and one death this morning, and that I would take him up to the camp at seven tomorrow. Voss said Dr. Brenner would want to rest after the journey. I said so would the men.

memories.experienced: Evening surgery was small and ordinary, which I could have kissed it for. Old Herr Kessler with his corns, again, and a view on the weather. A girl of about twelve from the sawmill with a nosebleed that had stopped by the time she got to me. Snow was coming down past the window again, the fat wet kind that does not stay. Sanna had gone home at six.
memories.did: I pared Herr Kessler's corns and agreed that it would be a hard winter, since he was sure of it. I showed the sawmill girl how to pinch the soft part of her nose and lean forward, not back, and gave her a boiled sweet for doing it well. Afterwards I swept the waiting room myself and put potatoes in the stove ashes for supper and ate them with salt standing at the window.

memories.experienced: Teodor came by at nine with Mira's arithmetic book because she had left it in my waiting room on Sunday. He was hoarse and had a cough he kept swallowing. When I asked him to open his mouth he did not. He said, very evenly, 'You do it to everyone, Ines. You look at people as if you're writing them up. I came to bring a book.' Then he said he was sorry about the navvy, and he meant that too.
memories.did: I told him a cough in a schoolroom full of children was my business. He said it was his throat. I said something unkind about schoolteachers who think chalk dust is a medicine. He put the book on the counter and said goodnight and went out into the snow without his scarf, which I noticed and did not call after him about. I sat for a long time with the arithmetic book in my lap.

memories.experienced: Brenner came up to the camp at half past eight, not seven. He listened to three chests, pressed two bellies, looked at no tongues and asked no one what they drank. Then he announced in the doorway of bunkhouse two, for the men to hear, that it was mountain ague: 'Thin air, cold, exertion. Rest, warmth, a light diet. Nothing catching.' Stoll nodded along. A man had died of it thirty hours before.
memories.did: I asked him outside how many cases of ague he had seen that gave a man a belly like a drum and killed him in four days. He said I was not a fever specialist. I said neither was he, and that I had eleven pages of notes he was welcome to read. He declined. I told him if he stopped the quinine I would go on giving it at my own cost, and he said, 'As you like, Fraulein,' and walked off to Voss's office.

memories.experienced: I stopped at the bakery for bread because I had forgotten to eat. Otto Brandt was taking the second batch out, flour to the elbows, and the shop was the only warm place in town. He wrapped a rye loaf and two poppy rolls and would not let me pay for the rolls. While he wrapped he said Mila had been coughing at night again since the snow, 'the old dry one', and her mother was fretting.
memories.did: I asked whether she was feverish or only coughing, and whether she was short of breath climbing the stairs. He said only coughing, mostly. I told him to keep a pan of water steaming in her room and to send for me at once, day or night, if her lips went blue or she could not finish a sentence. I ate one of the rolls on the step outside. It was very good.

memories.experienced: Inspector Hale was waiting by the woodpile at the back of the clinic, where no one from the square could see him. He took his hat off in the cold. He said he was not asking about the fever. He wanted to know what injuries I had treated from the tunnel since August: burns, falls, men who had come over dizzy or with headaches after a shift. He said, 'Off the record, Doctor. For now.'
memories.did: I brought him into the dispensary and read him from the casebook: the crushed finger Voss paid cash for, the four from the heading collapse, and the burned hand, Anton Reis, a shot-firer. I did not tell him about the lamp locked in my dispensary press with its gauze crimped wrong. I wanted to know first what he would do with it. I asked him why dizziness. He said, 'Because gas does that before it does anything else,' and thanked me, and left by the lane.

memories.experienced: Lotte came in after supper to help roll bandages, which she does now without being asked. She was quick at it and quiet. When I told her about the hospital letter she stopped rolling and said, 'You'd go?' and then, 'Of course you'd go. It's a real post.' A little later a boy from the Hart brought her a note from the innkeeper about her bill; she put it in her apron without reading it.
memories.did: I said I had not decided anything. She said the city was not as nice as I remembered, and did not say how she knew. I asked, carefully, whether she was all right for money at the Hart. She said yes, too quickly. We rolled forty bandages between us and I walked her back across the square because it was icy, and she held my arm the whole way.

memories.experienced: A plain Friday morning surgery. The postman, Wirth, with his bad knee, which he blames on dogs. A young mother with a baby who would not feed on the left side; the baby was fine and she was exhausted. A lumberman with a split scalp from a branch, bleeding theatrically all over Sanna's clean floor. Outside the snow had gone to slush and the gutters were running.
memories.did: I put five stitches in the lumberman's scalp while he sang to keep himself brave. I showed the young mother how to hold the baby in the rugby way on the left side and it latched in a minute; she cried, and I told her that was allowed. I told Wirth to stop kicking dogs and his knee would improve. Sanna and I ate bread and dripping at eleven and argued about whether to buy more carbolic.

memories.experienced: Eleven cases at the camp now. Two new overnight, both from bunkhouse four, and one of the early ones, the Tyrolean, sitting up asking for soup, which was the first good thing all week. Brenner's orders were pinned to the door of each bunkhouse: rest, warm flannel, beef tea. Someone had written 'and prayer' underneath in pencil. The quinine I had left would last perhaps four more days.
memories.did: I wrote all eleven into a table in the casebook: bunkhouse, bed, work gang, shift, onset day. Four from bunkhouse two, three from four, two from one, one each from five and six. It made no pattern I could see and I stared at it anyway. I gave quinine only to the four with the highest temperatures now, to stretch it, and hated choosing. I told the Tyrolean he could have soup if he drank two cups of boiled water first.

memories.experienced: I went to the schoolhouse at four, after the children had gone. Teodor was wiping the board. The sparrow was in its shoebox by the stove, where I had carried it on Tuesday, its wing still bound, eating crumbs. He had pinned up the pupils' compositions and Mira's was among them, titled 'My Aunt', three lines long: 'My aunt is a doctor. She has cold hands. She fixed a bird.' He still sounded hoarse.
memories.did: I said I was sorry for the chalk-dust remark and that he was right, I do look at people as if I am writing them up, and that it was the only way I knew to look after anyone. He said he knew, and that he would rather be looked after than written up. I asked if I could see his throat now, as a friend. He laughed and opened his mouth. Red, no spots. I told him honey and to shut up for two days. He wrote 'no' on the board.

memories.experienced: I went into the Lantern for a glass of schnapps on the way home because I wanted to be among people who were not sick. Jakob Stoll was at the corner table under the lamp with the gas log open in front of him, the black book with the company stamp. He had a second sheet beside it, loose and folded, and he was copying from it into the book line by line, looking from one to the other, licking his pencil.
memories.did: I stood at the bar with my back half-turned and watched him in the mirror behind the bottles for as long as the schnapps lasted. He filled most of a page. When he saw me he closed the book on the loose sheet and nodded, and I nodded back and said, 'Evening, Stoll. Late for paperwork.' He said the day's figures had to be written up clean. I paid and left, and wrote the time, ten past nine, in the back of my casebook when I got in.

memories.experienced: The quick way home from the Lantern is down Mill Lane and I took it without thinking. The old surgery was dark, the shutters nailed, the four screw holes still in the stone where my brass plate used to hang. There was new snow on the step that no one had walked on. I could smell wet ash from somewhere. My heart did the stupid thing it always does there.
memories.did: I did not stop and I did not look at the window of the operating room. I counted my steps to the corner, the way I did the first year, forty-two. At home I did not sleep. I lay and thought of Petr Anko's face under the chloroform, eleven years old, and the moment his pulse went, and how certain I had been of the appendix. Stoll's pencil and Petr's pulse got mixed up together, and at three I got up and made tea.

memories.experienced: Brenner came to the clinic at ten, in the camel coat, and asked Sanna for 'the lady doctor'. In my dispensary he said the company would be grateful if I stopped visiting the camp, as two physicians giving 'contradictory advice' unsettled the men. He also said Herr Voss was concerned about 'loose talk of contagion' reaching the railway. He wanted, he said, to see my notes, to form his own view.
memories.did: I told him he could read my casebook in my dispensary any time, but it would not leave the building, and that I would keep visiting the camp because the men were also residents of this parish and some of them were my patients before he got off the train. He said that was not my decision. I said it was not his either; the men could send for whom they liked. He did not open the casebook. Sanna shut the door behind him rather hard.

memories.experienced: Errands in the rain. My left boot had been letting water in since Tuesday and the cobbler on Kirchgasse, Haas, turned it over and showed me the sole worn through like paper. The market was half empty; the cabbage woman had come up from the valley anyway and was selling them two for a heller because no one else had come. A dog followed me for three streets.
memories.did: I left the boot with Haas and borrowed a pair of his old ones, two sizes too big, and stuffed the toes with newspaper. I bought four cabbages and a string of onions and paid the last of my small coins. I gave the dog the end of a sausage, which was a mistake, as it then followed me home and sat on the clinic step until Sanna threw water near it.

memories.experienced: Otto Brandt came running at half past four without his coat. Mila was worse. Upstairs over the bakery she was propped on three pillows, pulling at the air with her shoulders, lips dusky at the edges, and I could hear the wheeze from the doorway. Her pulse was a hundred and forty. Her mother was holding a basin and crying without any noise. Mila said, 'Hello, Doctor,' in two goes.
memories.did: I sat her forward over a pillow on a chair back, opened the window a crack and had Otto bring the big kettle up and set it steaming on a brazier by the bed. I gave her a quarter-dose of ipecac to loosen the chest and a little brandy in hot water. I told her mother to stop crying where Mila could see and she went out to do it on the stairs. I sent a boy for Sanna to hold the clinic and said I was staying the night.

memories.experienced: The night at the Brandts' was long. Around one the wheeze got tighter and Mila started to panic, which made it worse. At three she was blue round the mouth and I thought, very clearly, that I was going to lose a child in a room with a lamp in it again. Then she coughed up a great plug of mucus into the basin and took a whole breath. Otto was asleep in the chair by the door with flour still in his eyebrows.
memories.did: I held her hands and breathed slowly with her, out-two-three-four, until she copied me. I kept the kettle going and changed the hot flannels on her back every half hour. I counted her breaths on my watch every fifteen minutes and wrote them on the back of a flour bag: forty-eight, forty-four, then thirty-six after the plug came up. She was so like Mira in the lamplight, the same age near enough, the same fringe, that I had to stop looking at her face.

memories.experienced: By six Mila's fever had broken and she was asleep on her side, breathing twenty-eight a minute, pink again. The bakery ovens were being lit under us and the whole house smelled of wood smoke and yeast. Otto woke up ashamed of having slept and would not stop apologising. Her mother came in with coffee and put her forehead against my shoulder for a moment and said nothing.
memories.did: I listened to Mila's chest once more, still some crackle low on the right, and told her parents to keep the kettle steaming for three days, no school till I said so, and that I would come at noon and at night. I copied the breathing counts off the flour bag into the casebook when I got home. Otto sent me off with two loaves and a plaited sweet bread that I could not have refused with a gun to my head.

memories.experienced: At noon Lotte and Mira came to the clinic with soup from the Hart because Sanna had told the whole square I had been up all night. Mira asked, in a very small voice, whether Mila Brandt was going to die, because Mila sat in front of her at school and had lent her a blue crayon. Lotte had a new cuff on her sleeve, buttoned tight. She said the innkeeper had been asking about the bill.
memories.did: I told Mira no, Mila was not going to die, she was sleeping and pink and cross about missing school, and that she could make her a card. Mira said she would draw the bird on it. I gave her a sheet of my good writing paper and my pencil and she drew at my desk for twenty minutes while Lotte and I ate the soup. I did not ask about the bill, and I did not ask about the cuff.

memories.experienced: Up at the camp in the afternoon: still eleven cases, no new ones in a day and a half, three sitting up. Anton Reis caught me by the tool shed, his hand healed shiny and tight. He said Stoll had docked a day's pay from every sick man for 'malingering', on Brenner's word that it was only ague. He also said, looking at the portal and not at me, 'You should come up the heading some day and have a smell, Doctor.'
memories.did: I told Anton to tell the sick men I would write a note for any of them who wanted to take the docked pay to the mayor. I asked him what he meant about the smell and he said, 'Nothing you'd put in a book,' and went back to work. I gave out the last quinine to the two worst and counted what was left in Grete's box: enough for perhaps three days. On the way down I kept thinking about what else in that ground the tunnel might be letting out.

memories.experienced: Sunday night. The week's figures sat in front of me in the casebook: eleven fever cases, one dead, Pavel Hruby, nineteen; three recovering. Mila Brandt's chest through a bad night. Stoll copying figures into the gas log at a pub table I had not been meant to see. The hospital letter was on the blotter again. Wind in the stovepipe. Church bells had rung at six for evening prayer and I had not gone.
memories.did: I wrote a reply to the Municipal Hospital, a good one, accepting in principle and asking whether the post could begin later than spring. Then I read it back and it sounded like someone else, so I folded it into the casebook between the week's pages and did not seal it. I wrote on a slip, 'Answer by 4 December,' and pinned it over my desk. Then I went to bed and slept, for once, all the way to seven.

memories.experienced: Sanna had the kettle on before seven and the overnight slate on the table: three new fever cases sent down from the camp in the small hours, all navvies, all with the same heat and the same cramping gut. One of them, a Slovene called Matej, had a pulse of 118 and a tongue like old leather. The waiting room already smelled of wet wool and carbolic. Sanna said the camp runner had told her there would be more by noon, as if he were reporting the weather.
memories.did: I examined all three, wrote them into my casebook as cases twelve, thirteen and fourteen, and started a new column I should have started a week ago: which bunkhouse each man slept in. Matej was bunkhouse two, the others one and four. I told Sanna, "From now on nobody leaves this room without telling us where he sleeps and where he drinks." She wrote BUNK + WATER on the slate in capitals and underlined it twice. I gave each man ten grains of quinine and counted what was left in the jar.

memories.experienced: Mila Brandt was sitting up in the bed behind the bakery with a slate on her knees, doing sums. Her colour was better than the night I sat with her; the crackle at the base of the right lung had thinned to a faint rasp, and she only coughed twice while I listened. Otto Brandt hovered in the doorway with flour to the elbows and said she had eaten a whole roll that morning, the first in four days. The whole house smelled of rye and caraway.
memories.did: I counted her breaths, thirty to the minute, down from forty, and told Otto to keep the steam kettle going at night and to keep her home from school until Monday week. He tried to pay me and I said the account could wait, which is a stupid thing for a woman in my position to say. He pressed two loaves and a bag of rolls on me instead and I took them, because bread is at least not a debt to Grete.

memories.experienced: The afternoon was ordinary, which I have learned to be grateful for. A porter from the goods yard came in holding his ankle like a baby; he had stepped off a wagon backwards. Then old Frau Weiss with her leg ulcer, who told me for the fourth time that her late husband never needed a doctor in his life, and died at fifty-one. Rain came across the valley at three and rattled the dispensary window for an hour.
memories.did: I strapped the porter's ankle, told him it was a sprain and not a break, and said if he walked on it before Thursday I would hear about it from the whole yard. He laughed. I cleaned and dressed Frau Weiss's ulcer with zinc and told her that her husband had also never had anyone to tell him to sit down. She said I was cheeky and brought me a jar of plum jam anyway. I ate a roll of Otto's standing at the window.

memories.experienced: Supper at the Hart: dumplings and a thin gravy. Mira sat beside her mother and showed me her copybook without being asked, a page of joined-up letters and, in the margin, a bird with both wings drawn very carefully. Halfway through, a drover in the taproom shouted and slammed his tankard down, and Lotte's whole body went still, fork in the air, before she laughed it off. Mira did not look up at the noise. She looked at her mother.
memories.did: I told Mira her letters were neater than mine, which is true and not difficult. She said, "Mister Lind says yours are a disgrace," and I said Mister Lind had never had to write in a moving ship. That got nearly a smile. Afterwards, on the stairs, I asked Lotte quietly whether she was all right. She said, "It's only noise, Ines," and went up with Mira before I could say anything else.

memories.experienced: The camp sick-tent held nine men on straw pallets under grey blankets, and the smell of it met me thirty yards down the path. Dr. Brenner was already there in his city boots, taking temperatures with a glass thermometer he wiped on his sleeve. He told me the new cases were "exactly as expected in mountain ague" and that rest and a little quinine would see them through. Two of the men were talking nonsense with fever. One had soiled himself.
memories.did: I asked Brenner how many grains he was giving and he said five, twice a day. I told him that was not enough to cool a cat. He said the company's stores were not bottomless. I went down the row with my own jar, dosed the three worst properly, and wrote their bunkhouses into my casebook again: two from one, one from two. Before leaving I made the orderly boil the drinking bucket, which Brenner called "theatrical".

memories.experienced: Grete's shop was warm and smelled of camphor and liquorice. She had the ledger open on the counter before I reached it, my page, the column of figures in her small upright hand. She said she had four ounces of quinine sulphate in from the Linz wholesaler and I could have three of them, but that she was writing every grain down. She also asked, not unkindly, whether I had answered the city hospital yet.
memories.did: I took the three ounces and watched her write it in: quinine, 3 oz, on account, 30th. My page now ran to the bottom and over. I said, "You'll have it all, Grete, when the company pays me for the fever work." She said the company had not paid anyone for anything since August. On the way home I thought about the hospital letter in my desk drawer and what a salaried post would do to that page, and then felt cheap for thinking it.

memories.experienced: Father Kurz caught me outside the post office with his umbrella and his news. The man from the railway, he said, meaning the inspector, was still lodging at the Hart and ate alone and tipped badly. The Hart's girl was walking out with a brakeman. And had I finished with the old map yet, because the bishop's secretary liked to count the vestry's things at Advent and he would rather not explain.
memories.did: I told him the map was safe in my desk, wrapped in oilcloth, and that I was still reading it. He asked what a doctor wanted with mine galleries and I said I liked to know what was under my feet, which is true enough. I promised it back before Advent. He patted my arm and said Lotte looked better lately, and I said nothing, which he took as confirmation of something.

memories.experienced: Teodor was stacking slates when I came by the schoolhouse at four. The stove had gone out and the room smelled of chalk and wet coats. He showed me Mira's composition, 'A Person I Know': three lines about her aunt, who 'mends people with thread and is not frightened of blood but is frightened of cats.' He said she had asked him how to spell 'frightened' twice and would not let him see it until it was finished.
memories.did: I said I was not frightened of cats, I simply disliked them on principle. He laughed at me. I asked if I could keep the page and he said no, it was hers, but he would ask her. We walked as far as the bridge together. After our row last week I was careful with him, and he noticed, and said, "You can stop being polite to me, Ines, it doesn't suit you." I went home smiling like an idiot.

memories.experienced: A farmer's wife from the upper road, Frau Moser, came in at eight with a hot, hard breast, three weeks after her fourth child, and a husband who waited outside because he said it was women's business. It was early mastitis, not yet an abscess. The baby, brought along in a basket, screamed the whole time with the lungs of a foreman. The sky was clear for once and the ridge looked close enough to touch.
memories.did: I showed her how to keep feeding from that side, hot cloths before, cabbage leaves after, and gave her a powder for the fever. I told her husband through the door that his wife was to do no washing for a week and that if I heard otherwise I would come and do it myself in front of the neighbours. Sanna wrote her up while I fed the baby a finger of sugar water to shut it up.

memories.experienced: At twenty to five the camp bell started ringing and did not stop. From the clinic step I could see black smoke rising below the portal. By the time I got up the track with my bag, bunkhouse three was burning end to end, the tar-paper roof curling off in sheets. Stoll was running a bucket chain from the lower trough, bellowing. Voss stood by the timber stack in his shirtsleeves, giving orders nobody could hear.
memories.did: I found where they had laid the hurt men on the grass: two burned, several coughing from smoke. I shouted at Stoll to keep his chain away from them and he told me where to go, then did it. Watching him swing buckets I thought, absurdly, of him in the pub copying one page of the gas log onto another, calm as a clerk. I asked Voss for a cart. He gave me one without argument, which I noted.

memories.experienced: We brought the two burned men down to the clinic in the cart. Wenzel Haas had burns across both forearms and the backs of his hands where he had dragged a bunkmate out; the skin had blistered and split. Dimitri Lukas, the bunkmate, was burned across the back and thighs, the shirt cooked into him. He kept apologising in three languages. The waiting room smelled of scorched wool for hours.
memories.did: Sanna cut Dimitri's shirt away with the curved scissors while I gave both men a quarter grain of morphia. We soaked the cloth off in warm saline, cleaned the burns, dressed them in carron oil and lint and bandaged loosely. I wrote Wenzel's hands as partial thickness and Dimitri's back as partial with two deep patches the size of a palm. I told Wenzel he was a fool and a hero and that the two were usually the same man.

memories.experienced: By dusk the bunkhouse was a black frame, steaming. The men were saying someone had set it, the Italians, or the Slovaks, depending who was talking. Anton Reis found me by the ruins and took me round to the stove end: the iron flue had cracked at the collar and a row of wet socks and trousers had been hung on a line a foot from it. The planking there was burned deepest. Hale was standing a little way off, listening.
memories.did: I crouched and looked at the flue and the char pattern and told Anton he was right, it started at the stove. I said it loudly enough for the men near us to hear: "Nobody set this. A cracked pipe and wet socks." Hale came over and asked whether the two burned men were tunnel crew. I said yes, both on the heading gang, and that they would not be working for a month. He wrote it in a small notebook.

memories.experienced: Lotte came to the clinic after ten with a covered pot of soup from the Hart's kitchen and found me at the desk still writing up the fire. She said Mira was asleep and the innkeeper's wife was listening for her. She sat across from me while I ate, and twice she took a breath as though she were about to say something, and twice she let it go and asked instead about the burned men.
memories.did: I ate the whole pot, barley and ham, and told her about Wenzel dragging his bunkmate out. I finished the casebook entry with soup on my fingers. When she took the third breath I put the pen down and said, "Lotte. Whatever it is." She said, "Not tonight," and kissed the top of my head, which she has not done since she was fifteen, and went back down the lane with the empty pot.

memories.experienced: First dressing change on the burned men at seven. Wenzel's hands were weeping but pink under the blisters, no smell. Dimitri had slept on his belly and his back looked angrier, but his temperature was only 99.4. He asked if he would be scarred and I said yes, and he said good, his girl in Maribor would believe the story. Sanna had been up twice in the night to turn him.
memories.did: I soaked the lint off in warm saline and redressed both of them with fresh carron oil, and told Sanna she was to go and sleep until noon, which she ignored. I made Dimitri drink two pints of weak tea with salt and sugar before I would let him have a cigarette at the window. In the casebook I drew the two deep patches on his back as outlines so I could compare them tomorrow.

memories.experienced: The camp clerk was rehousing the men from bunkhouse three and had a list of every bunk in the camp pinned to his hut wall, with names and a small well symbol beside each house: bunkhouses one, two and four draw from the upper well by the spoil heap; five, six and the old three from the lower spring. He was putting the burned-out men into bunkhouse one. I laid my casebook beside his list.
memories.did: I went through every fever case I had, nineteen, against his bunks. Sixteen slept in one, two or four. Of the other three, two worked the heading and ate at the upper cookhouse, which fills its kettles from the same well. I copied his list out in full while he watched. I asked him to hold off moving the new men into bunkhouse one, and he said the company told him where men went, not the doctor.

memories.experienced: Haas the cobbler on Kirchgasse had my left boot ready at last, five days after he had turned it over in his doorway and looked at the sole as if it had personally offended him. He said the winter would be a hard one because his knee said so, and his knee had been right in '98. While he tacked the last of the new half-sole on I sat on his bench in one stocking, his old boot on the other foot, and listened to a canary in the back room.
memories.did: I paid him forty heller, which he said was the doctor's price and I said was robbery, and we were both pleased. I gave him back his old boots with the newspaper still in the toes. I asked after his knee professionally and he refused to let me look at it. I walked home on dry feet for the first time in a week, bought a newspaper I did not read, and left it on the clinic table for the patients.

memories.experienced: At the station to collect a crate of lint and bandage from the noon train, I found Emil Ott supervising the unloading of two big iron pumps marked for the contractor. He said they were the second pair since the middle of last month. The heading, he said, was taking water "like a sieve since it went past the red rock" and they were pumping day and night into the drain down the slope. He said it the way he says everything, as a small fact he has kept for you.
memories.did: I signed for my crate and asked him when the water had started. He thought about it and said the second week of October, near enough, because that was when they ordered the first pumps. I asked where the drain ran and he pointed up at the ridge and said, "Down past the camp, doctor, where else?" I carried the crate home thinking about water finding its way downhill.

memories.experienced: After supper I spread the vestry map on the dispensary table under the lamp, weighted with two jars. The old galleries ran out from the adit above town in brown ink, with shafts marked as little squares and the 1891 fall hatched over in red with a date and a cross. I laid the tunnel line across it from the company's printed notice. The two lines crossed under the ridge, west of the portal, above where the camp sits.
memories.did: I measured with a ruler and my thumb and worked out that the heading could have reached the lower end of Gallery Two early last month, which is exactly when Ott's pumps started. I pencilled a faint line on tracing paper, not on the map, from the crossing point down to the upper well. I thought about the eleven men under that hatching and about water standing in those galleries since 1891. I went to bed and did not sleep much.

memories.experienced: I was at the upper well by half past six with four clean jars. The bucket came up cold and the water in it was faintly cloudy, a yellowish haze that settled slowly. It tasted of iron and something like bad eggs, and when I put my nose to the jar it smelled exactly as a cellar smells, wet stone and old timber: the smell of a mine. The lower spring, which I sampled after, was clear and tasted of nothing at all.
memories.did: I filled and labelled two jars from each source, UPPER and LOWER with the date and hour, and held them side by side against the sunrise so I could see the difference plainly. I spat the water out and rinsed my mouth from my own flask. A cook's boy came up with two buckets and I told him to fetch his water from the lower spring today, and gave him a sweet to make it an order.

memories.experienced: Anton was at the portal coming off the night shift, and he walked me along the drain. It was a timber flume carrying orange-brown water from the heading down the slope and discharging into a gully that ran above the upper well. In the silt were splinters of black, rotten pit props. Anton said, "That's not our timber. We broke into the old workings on the ninth of October. Water came in like a tap. Stoll said keep quiet about it or the mine company's heirs would be at the contractor for years."
memories.did: I picked a piece of the old prop out of the silt and wrapped it in my handkerchief. I asked Anton exactly where they had broken through and he drew it for me in the mud with a stick; it matched the crossing on my tracing of the map almost to the yard. I followed the gully down on my own feet to where it soaked into the ground forty yards above the well-head. I said to Anton, "They're drinking the mine."

memories.experienced: I found Brenner in the sick-tent and set my four jars on his table in a row. He held the UPPER jar to the light, sniffed it, and said mountain water always tasted of rock, that ague came from altitude and damp air, and that I had no apparatus to test anything. He said Mr. Voss would not close the only near well on the ridge "on a country doctor's nose", and nor would he recommend it.
memories.did: I told him sixteen of nineteen cases slept by that well and showed him the clerk's list and the old prop. I said, "Your ague has a postal address." He said my figures proved only that more men lived at the top of the camp. I asked him, very quietly, to put in writing that he had been shown the water and declined. He would not. Walking down I thought about who sits above a company doctor, and it was the mayor, who wants the tunnel more than anyone.

memories.experienced: Lotte came at nine, alone, and sat in the patients' chair with her coat on. She told me in a flat voice, like a list, about Friedrich: the drinking that started with the business going under, the first time he hit her, two years ago at Easter, the rib that was broken in March, and the debts, nearly two thousand three hundred crowns, to men who came to the door. Then she took a folded letter out of her glove and gave it to me.
memories.did: I read it twice by the lamp. It was his hand, careful and sober: she was to come home by the first of December, the girl belonged in her father's house, and if she did not come he would come for Mira himself. I said, "He can't have her. He can't have either of you." I asked to see her ribs and she let me, and I felt the old callus on the left seventh. I held her hand for a long time without saying anything useful.

memories.experienced: Lotte asked me what she should do with the letter. She said it had come to the Hart on the thirteenth of October, the day I walked in on her with the scarf, and that she had read it every night after Mira was asleep, and hidden it in her glove, her Bible, once in Mira's boot. She said she was sick of its weight. The stove in the dispensary was still hot from the day. It was nearly eleven.
memories.did: I said, "We could burn it, if you want to. It's yours to say." She thought and said yes. I opened the stove door and she put it in herself, and we watched the envelope go brown, then the pages curl. I told her I would remember the date, the demand, the threat against Mira, word for word, in case anyone ever needed them, and I wrote them in the back of my casebook when she had gone. I walked her to the Hart door.

memories.experienced: At the Hart at seven Lotte was at the breakfast table with her hair down and colour in her face. She said she had slept seven hours straight, which she had not done since March. Mira had already gone off to school with the innkeeper's boy. The taproom was empty and the landlord was sanding the floor. Lotte said, quietly, "I kept waiting to feel worse for telling you. I don't."
memories.did: I sat with her over coffee and did not ask anything. I told her that if Friedrich ever came up the line, Emil Ott would know before he was off the platform and so would I, and that there were rooms above the clinic not doing anything useful. She said, "Let's not be sisters too fast, Ines." I laughed, which I had not expected to do. I checked her forearm, where the last of the bruises had gone, and left her half my rolls.

memories.experienced: The morning list ran to eleven. A boy of twelve with a fish hook through the pad of his thumb, which his father had tried to pull out backwards. A carter with a molar abscess who had been drinking schnapps against it since Friday. A colicky infant, a sore back, two coughs, and a woman who wanted a tonic for her husband's temper, which I do not stock. Fresh snow showed white on the top of the ridge.
memories.did: I pushed the hook through, snipped the barb and backed it out, and the boy watched the whole thing and asked to keep it. I pulled the carter's tooth with Sanna holding his head and he fainted afterwards, not during. I told the woman there was no tonic for a temper but that she could send her husband to me and I would have a word. Sanna said the cobbler's knee had been right.

memories.experienced: I went to the schoolhouse at the noon break. The children were out in the yard shrieking. Teodor listened to the whole well business while eating an apple, then asked the right question: what would convince a mayor who wants a tunnel? He offered to draw the camp plan fair, bunkhouses, wells and every case marked, in his clean hand. Mira came in from the yard, red-cheeked, and stood at my elbow until I noticed her.
memories.did: I said yes to the plan and gave him the clerk's list and my figures. Mira asked, all in one breath, whether she could sleep at my house tonight because Mama said she had to ask me herself. I said yes before I could think of a reason not to. She said, "Can I see the bird bones?" and I said the skeleton was a sparrow, not her bird, and she said she knew. Teodor looked at me over her head as if I had passed an exam.

memories.experienced: Lotte brought Mira round at seven with a nightdress and a toothbrush in a cloth bag and a list of things Mira would not eat. Then she left, and it was just the two of us and the clinic after hours. Mira looked at everything: the sparrow skeleton in its case, the jars, the bone saw, which she asked about. At bedtime she asked whether my hands ever shook when I cut people. She fell asleep at twenty to ten.
memories.did: I made up the settle in my sitting room with the good blanket and my own pillow. I let her hold the sparrow skeleton over the table, in two hands. I told her the truth about my hands: that they shook afterwards, never during, and that that was the right way round. She thought about it and said, "Mama's shake before." I said nothing to that. I sat in the chair with a book I didn't read until she was asleep.

memories.experienced: At about three Mira cried out in her sleep and I was up before I knew it. She was sitting up on the settle, not quite awake, saying, "He broke the blue plate, he broke it." When she came round she was embarrassed and wanted the lamp. At breakfast she ate two slices of bread with Frau Weiss's plum jam and asked me to plait her hair because Mama always did it.
memories.did: I sat on the edge of the settle and held her until she was properly awake, and left the lamp turned low for the rest of the night. I did not ask about the plate or who had broken it; I knew. In the morning I plaited her hair and made a poor job of it, lumpy on the left. She looked in the dispensary mirror and said, "It's bad," and then, "I'll keep it." I walked her back to the Hart at eight, since it was Sunday.

memories.experienced: On the way back I cut through St. Veit's graveyard. Marta Anko was on her knees at the far wall, at Petr's grave, pulling dead leaves off the small stone with bare hands. She had a black shawl and a basket of late asters. She looked up and saw me at the gate, and for a moment neither of us moved. Then she turned back to the grave and bent lower, so that her back was to me.
memories.did: I stood at the gate longer than I should have. I thought of the boy on the table in the old surgery six years ago, the blood pressure falling under my hands and me not knowing why, and the question I never stop asking. I did not go in. I did not have anything to say that she would want. I went round by the lane instead of through the graves and walked the rest of the way faster than I needed to.

memories.experienced: Evening rounds at the camp: two new cases, a cook from the upper cookhouse and one of the men moved out of burned bunkhouse three into bunkhouse one three days ago. Twenty-one cases now, one dead, and nobody from the lower houses in over a week. The cook's boy had been drinking from the lower spring as I told him, and was well. The quinine jar in my bag was down to about forty grains.
memories.did: I dosed the two new men and wrote them up by lantern: case twenty, bunkhouse one; case twenty-one, upper cookhouse. That settled it for me. On the walk down I decided I would go to Mayor Dahl on Monday with Teodor's plan, my jars and my casebook, and ask Inspector Hale to come with me, since a mayor listens to the railway if not to me. I said out loud to nobody on the track, "Monday, then."

memories.experienced: Sanna had the night book open on the dispensary table when I came down at half past six. Two new fever cases overnight, both from the upper row of bunkhouses, both men who drew their water from the upper well. That made twenty-two of the twenty-three cases on that water. The kettle had boiled dry because she had forgotten it too. My jar of well water from Friday still stood on the sill, grey sediment settled into a finger-width band at the bottom, and it still smelled like a wet coin.
memories.did: I refilled the kettle and sat down with my casebook. I copied every fever case onto one sheet: name, bunkhouse, which well, day of onset. Twenty-two upper well, and one lower-row man who swore he drank only beer. I took the camp plan Teodor had drawn fair for me and put a cross on it for each man, and the crosses sat on the upper well like flies on jam. I told Sanna, 'This goes to the mayor today, not to Brenner. Brenner has had it twice.' She said the mayor would want it shorter. I said he would get it shorter from Hale.

memories.experienced: Hale was eating kippers in the front room of the Hart at nine, grey coat over the chair back, notebook beside the plate. He read my sheet all the way through without speaking, then turned the camp sketch sideways. He said the railway's regulations gave him standing on 'the health and safety of persons employed on the works', and that nobody had ever used that clause for water. He said, 'Brenner answers to the contractor. The mayor answers to the town. I answer to Parliament, in theory.'
memories.did: I stood because I did not want to be offered breakfast and have to say yes. I told him the well had to be shut today, not after another report, because the incubation seemed to be about a week and every day was seven more days. I asked him to come with me to Dahl at eleven. He wiped his fingers, said 'Eleven,' and wrote it down. I left before Lotte could come down the stairs and ask what I was doing at her inn with an inspector.

memories.experienced: Mayor Dahl kept us standing in his office above the post room for four minutes while he finished a letter. Then he said the contractor was already three weeks behind and he would not have a lady doctor's sums stop the works. Hale said nobody was stopping the works, only a well, and that if the camp's sickness reached the town the railway would have to consider whether Kessel Pass was a fit terminus. Dahl went pink at the neck. He said, 'Brenner says it's mountain ague.' Hale said, 'Brenner is wrong.'
memories.did: I put my sheet flat on his blotter and pointed at the twenty-two crosses. I said the town spring was clean and could fill two water carts a day for the camp, and I had already asked the carter what it would cost: eleven crowns a week. Dahl signed an order at twenty past eleven closing the upper camp well 'until further notice' and had his clerk make two copies. I took one. Outside on the steps I found my hands were shaking and I put them in my pockets so Hale would not see.

memories.experienced: The bakery was shutting when I got there at five, the windows fogged. Mila Brandt was on a stool behind the counter wrapping rolls in paper, and she coughed only twice while I watched, both times dry. Her father said she had slept through the last three nights without the kettle steaming by the bed. Her chest, when I listened in the back room, was clearer on the left than it had been in a month, a faint crackle at the right base still.
memories.did: I counted her breaths at twenty-two a minute and told Otto Brandt that was good, which it was. I told him to keep her out of the flour dust in the mornings and to keep the window cracked at night even though she would complain. Mila asked if she could go to the parents' evening at the school; I said that was her father's business but her lungs had no objection. Otto would not take money for the loaf he pushed at me. I ate half of it walking home.

memories.experienced: At the camp at eight the upper well already had three planks nailed across the mouth and a painted board: CLOSED BY ORDER. Stoll stood by it with his arms folded and told me his men had lost a morning carrying from the lower well. Then Brenner came down the path in his city boots, holding the mayor's order like something wet. He said, loud enough for the men to hear, 'You have gone over my head, Dr. Calder. That is not done between colleagues.'
memories.did: I said it was done between colleagues when one of them had been wrong for a fortnight with a navvy in the ground to show for it. That was unkind and I did not take it back. I told him the water cart from the town spring would come at ten and at four and that anyone who drank from the lower well should boil it. Stoll spat and said doctors did not dig tunnels. I said no, but we got the men after the tunnel was done with them.

memories.experienced: Ordinary surgery hours, and I was grateful for every dull minute of them. A woodcutter from the upper farms with a split thumb he had bound in a sock for two days. Old Frau Lechner with her bunions and her opinions about the new priest's sermons, which were Father Kurz's sermons, as they had been for twenty years. A clerk from the station with a stye. Sanna hummed something from the church choir while she boiled the instruments, badly, and the waiting room smelled of wet wool.
memories.did: I cleaned the thumb, put in four stitches, and told the woodcutter a sock was not a dressing and to come back Friday. I cut Frau Lechner's corn and did not argue about sermons. I gave the clerk a warm compress and told him not to squeeze it. At noon I ate bread and cheese standing at the dispensary counter and wrote the three of them up in the day book. Sanna asked if I wanted the afternoon off. I said I did, and then saw two more.

memories.experienced: The crate from the city had come on the noon train and Grete had it open on her counter when I went in: two ounces of quinine sulphate and a hundred fever powders, the first full delivery since the outbreak began. She ran her finger down her ledger and turned it around so I could read my line: two hundred and twenty-nine crowns, now two hundred and sixty-one with the crate. She said, 'I hear you shut the well. I hear it from three people.'
memories.did: I said I would not need half the quinine if the well had been the thing, and that I would send back what I did not open. She said she would not take it back, the stuff kept, and the next fever would not ask permission. I paid her twelve crowns in coins, which was the week's cash from the camp. I asked her to write it in front of me. She did, in her small square hand, and said, 'Sit down before you fall down,' and gave me a glass of her cherry cordial.

memories.experienced: Lotte brought Mira to the clinic for supper at six, a pot of lentils wrapped in a towel. Mira had a new drawing: the schoolhouse with every window lit and a stick-man at the door with enormous spectacles, which she said was Herr Lind. She wanted to know how I knew a man was sick before he told me. She watched my hands the whole meal. Lotte was quieter than usual and kept looking at the stairs, the way she has since the letter burned.
memories.did: After supper I sat Mira on the examining couch and showed her how to find a pulse at the wrist with two fingers, not the thumb, because the thumb has its own. I timed her against my watch: ninety-four, fast because she was excited. Then she took mine and got seventy-one and was furious I was so slow. I told her slow was a doctor's privilege. Lotte laughed out loud for the first time all evening. I walked them back to the Hart at eight with a lamp.

memories.experienced: A farmer's wife brought her boy in at eight with his hand clamped over his left ear and his face blotched from crying. Pain for two days, worse lying down, a fever of a hundred and one. The drum was red and bulging when I looked. Outside it had started to rain, fine and steady, the kind that comes off the ridge and does not stop until evening. Sanna reported the coal man had short-weighted us again, which she discovered by weighing it.
memories.did: I told the mother it was an ordinary ear infection and not the camp fever, which is what she had come to ask. I gave her warm oil drops and a powder for the pain and told her the ear might burst and weep, and that if it did the pain would ease and she should not panic. I charged her one crown and took eggs instead. I told Sanna to keep the short sack by the door and I would show it to the coal man myself.

memories.experienced: The fever bunkhouse at the camp held nine men at noon, down from fourteen on Monday. Three new cases since the well was shut, all men who had drunk from it the week before; the last, a young Tyrolean called Brugger, had been poorly since Saturday, his mates said, before the planks went on. The water cart had come at ten as promised, and the men were queueing with buckets. The two burned men from bunkhouse three were up and walking, hands still dressed. The place smelled of carbolic and wet boots.
memories.did: I went down the row with my thermometer and my notebook. Six of the nine were below a hundred. I dosed Brugger with quinine from the new tin and told the orderly to sponge him every two hours. I counted the remaining powders in the ward box, forty-one, and wrote it down. I asked the queue at the water cart whether anyone was still drinking from the upper well through the planks; a boy admitted he had tried. I told him the planks were there to save his guts, and made him show me his tongue.

memories.experienced: Someone knocked at the back door at a quarter to eleven, three knocks and then one. It was Anton Reis, rain dripping off his cap, his healed hand pale in the lamplight. He would not come further than the scullery. He said, low, 'Stoll keeps two books. The true one's under his mattress in the foreman's hut, green cloth cover, wrapped in oilcloth. The black company book in the lamp room is the one he shows the inspector. Same numbers every shift in the black one. The green one doesn't agree.'
memories.did: I asked him how he knew. He said he had seen Stoll copying from one to the other on a Sunday, the way I had seen him at the pub. I asked if the green book showed gas at the face; he said it showed enough that they should have stopped twice in October. I asked if he would say so to Hale. He said no, he had a mother in Linz and a job. I promised I would not use his name if I could help it. He left by the yard gate without a lamp.

memories.experienced: I could not get back to sleep. The rain drummed on the lean-to roof and the stove ticked as it cooled. From the window I could see a single lamp at the tunnel portal, which meant the night shift was in. The letter from the city hospital was still in the top drawer of the desk, where it had been since the end of October. Somewhere down the lane a dog barked at nothing for a quarter of an hour.
memories.did: I got up and rolled clean bandages, forty yards of them, because my hands wanted a job. I ate a slice of bread with dripping standing at the stove. I took the hospital letter out and read the salary line again, two hundred and eighty crowns a month and rooms, then put it back without reading the rest. I thought about Anton walking home in the rain without a lamp and about which book the men at the face were trusting their lives to. At two I gave up and made tea.

memories.experienced: Hale was in the station waiting room at seven, waiting for the down train to the valley and back. Emil Ott brought us two cups of coffee without being asked and stayed nearer the stove than he needed to. Hale listened to me without writing anything at first. Then he wrote three lines. He said, 'A second book is a serious charge. If I walk into that hut without cause and find nothing, Voss has me recalled in a week, and the book goes in the stove.'
memories.did: I told him what I had been told: two books, a green one under the foreman's mattress and the black company one in the lamp room, the numbers not agreeing. I did not give Anton's name; I said a man at the face. Hale did not ask for it, which I liked. I reminded him that I had seen Stoll copying at the pub with my own eyes. He asked me not to go near the foreman's hut and not to say a word in town. I said I was a doctor, not a fool, and drank Ott's coffee, which was terrible.

memories.experienced: The Egger farm sent the boy down at ten: his mother's waters had gone at dawn and the midwife from Oberau was snowed in on the other side of the col. The farmhouse kitchen was hot as a forge. It was her fourth, and she was calmer than her husband, who kept offering me schnapps. The baby came at twenty to two, a girl, face up, cord once round the neck, and she screamed the moment I had it off.
memories.did: I slipped the cord over her head with one finger, delivered the shoulders, and handed her to her mother still slippery. I waited for the afterbirth, checked it whole, and massaged the belly until it firmed. I weighed the baby on the kitchen scale in a flour sack: seven pounds and a bit. I drank one schnapps to stop the husband offering. They asked what the town doctor's name was because they wanted to use it; I told them to name her after the midwife, who would be more offended.

memories.experienced: Father Kurz was in the vestry polishing the candlesticks when I brought back the mine map at five. He unrolled it on the vestment chest and put his thumb exactly on the lower end of Gallery Two, just short of the hatched square of the 1891 fall, where my pencil had pressed through the tracing paper onto his linen. He said, 'You've been writing on my map, Doctor.' Then he said the whole parish knew Teodor Lind had asked me to speak at the parents' evening on Saturday, and wasn't that nice.
memories.did: I apologised for the pencil and rubbed it out with my handkerchief. I showed him where the tunnel drainage must have broken into that gallery and why the water had run down to the upper camp well, and he listened properly, the gossip gone out of his face for a minute. I asked him whether the mine captain who left it to the parish had drawn it himself; he did not know. On the parents' evening I said Herr Lind had asked me to talk about boiling water, which is not romantic. He said, 'Nothing is, until it is,' and rolled the map back into its tube.

memories.experienced: Teodor was at the clinic door at a quarter past seven with a bundle of exercise books under his arm, as if he had come about work. He had. He wanted to know whether I would still speak on Saturday, twenty minutes, on boiling water and washing hands, because half the parents had men at the camp. He said Mira had read aloud in class for the first time, a whole page, and had stopped only once, at 'Kessel'. He looked at me a little too long over that.
memories.did: I said yes, twenty minutes, and that I would bring the jar of well water because a jar of grey water was better than any speech. I told him I was glad about Mira, and that she had taken my pulse on Tuesday and thought me dull. He laughed. I did not ask him in, because Sanna was still in the dispensary and would have made tea and then a face at me. I said goodnight on the step and then stood in the hall for a while doing nothing at all.

memories.experienced: Konrad Voss came to the clinic at eleven in a good overcoat, carrying a bottle of Kirschwasser and an envelope with the sixteen crowns still owed for Horn and Benes from the fall at the face. He was charming. He admired the new shelving. Then he said, 'You and the inspector have been having coffee, I hear. I'd hate to think a good doctor was being drawn into engineering matters she can't judge. The tunnel is my patient, Dr. Calder. I don't tell you how to set a bone.'
memories.did: I took the envelope and counted it in front of him, sixteen, and wrote him a receipt. I left the bottle on the counter unopened. I said the tunnel's men were my patients whether he liked it or not, and that I judged what came out of it on stretchers. He smiled and said he hoped we understood each other. I said I thought we did. I did not mention any book, and I kept my face still while I thought of the green one under Stoll's mattress. He tipped his hat to Sanna on the way out.

memories.experienced: When the door shut Sanna came out of the dispensary with a face like thunder and said she had heard every word through the partition. She said her brother had worked for a contractor like Voss on the Arlberg line and had been told the same thing about his own lungs. My hands were not quite steady when I went to write. The Kirschwasser sat on the counter catching the light like a bribe, which it was, with a label from a good distiller in Bludenz.
memories.did: I opened my casebook to the back pages where I keep things that are not cases and wrote down Voss's visit as close to word for word as I could manage, with the time, 11.05 to 11.20, and 'Sanna Feld present, heard through partition'. I underlined 'The tunnel is my patient'. I asked Sanna to initial it and she did. Then I gave her the bottle and told her to take it to her brother or pour it down the drain, whichever felt better.

memories.experienced: At the camp at three the fever bunkhouse had six men in it and none of them new. Brugger's fever had broken overnight; he was sitting up asking for sausage. The orderly's chart showed no fresh case since Brugger on Wednesday. The water cart came on time, and someone had painted a skull on the upper well board under CLOSED BY ORDER, which I felt was fair. Two of the lower-row men were back on shift and one waved his pick at me from the portal path.
memories.did: I took every temperature myself, not trusting the orderly's arithmetic, and wrote them down: all six under a hundred. I told Brugger he could have the sausage tomorrow and broth today. I counted the quinine left in the ward box, thirty-three powders, and took twenty back for the clinic. I told the orderly not to say 'over' to anyone yet, least of all the mayor, because I wanted a full week clean before I said it aloud. Walking back down I caught myself whistling.

memories.experienced: Supper alone: potato soup reheated from yesterday and the heel of the Brandts' loaf. Wind came up after dark and rattled the sash in the front room. The lamp needed trimming and smoked until I did it. My stockings had gone at both heels. From across the lane came the Gruber children practising something on a mouth organ, the same four notes over and over, and I realised I had been listening for footsteps on the step for a while.
memories.did: I darned both stockings, badly, with brown wool because the grey had run out. I trimmed the lamp. I wrote my notes for Saturday's talk on the back of an old prescription pad: boil for as long as it takes to say the Lord's Prayer twice, wash hands after the privy and before bread, and never trust water because it looks clear. I crossed out 'never trust water' as too gloomy for parents and then put it back in. I went to bed at ten and thought about the schoolteacher.

memories.experienced: Brenner came to the clinic at nine with his hat in his hands. He said the company was recalling him to the city as soon as their new man came up, in a fortnight or so. He said, stiffly, that the case numbers since the well closed were 'suggestive' and that he would be writing so in his report. Then he said, 'The navvy who died. Hruby. If it was the water, I should have seen it.' He looked older than he had in the camp, and smaller in my doorway.
memories.did: I gave him a chair and a cup of coffee, which I had not planned to do. I said I had not seen it either until the crosses were on paper, and that it was the drainage that found the old galleries, not either of us. I showed him the jar of water. He held it up to the window and said nothing for a while. I told him I would put in my notes that he had revised his opinion. He thanked me and shook my hand at the door.

memories.experienced: Afternoon surgery was the coal man, of all people, with a back molar gone black and his jaw swollen to the ear. He said nothing about short sacks and neither did I at first. The tooth came out in one piece on the second pull with a crack like a walnut. Outside, the first proper snow of the week began, big wet flakes that melted on the cobbles. Sanna had ironed my good blouse for tonight without asking and hung it on the dispensary door.
memories.did: I packed the socket with gauze and told him to bite down for an hour and not to drink spirits until tomorrow, which he received like a death sentence. Then I pointed at the short sack by the door and said the extraction was three crowns, less whatever the coal was light, which by Sanna's scale made it two. He paid two and did not argue. I thanked Sanna for the blouse and she said, 'It's for the parents, Doctor,' with no expression at all.

memories.experienced: The schoolhouse was full by seven, thirty-odd parents on children's benches with their knees up. Teodor had lit every lamp, like Mira's drawing. Lotte sat in the second row with Mira, who had her slate in her lap to show me her sums. Otto Brandt came in late with flour still on his cuffs and asked afterwards whether Mila could go back to school on Monday. Half the questions were from camp wives about the water cart, and one asked if the fever could come back.
memories.did: I talked for nineteen minutes and held up the jar of grey water at the start so they would stop looking at my blouse. I told them the Lord's Prayer twice was long enough to boil. I said the fever could come back if anyone pulled the planks off the upper well, and that I would know who. They laughed. I told Otto yes, Monday, if she stayed warm. Mira showed me eleven sums, all right, and I said so, and she let me hold her slate.

memories.experienced: When the parents had gone Lotte took Mira back to the Hart and gave me a look over her shoulder I did not care for. Teodor and I stacked the benches against the wall and he blew out the lamps one by one until only the one on his desk was left. He said, 'You were good. You were funny, which you never let yourself be.' He had chalk on his sleeve. He stood very close, and then he asked whether he could, and I said yes.
memories.did: I kissed him back, by the stove, with my coat half on. It lasted longer than I would have guessed and afterwards I laughed, which was not the reaction he expected, and I had to explain it was because I had been thinking about it since Tuesday and it had been simpler than thinking. He said he had been thinking since the quarrel. I said we were both idiots. I let him walk me home in the snow and did not ask him in, and at the door I kissed him once more.

memories.experienced: Sanna arrived at eight, though it was Sunday, and stopped in the doorway of the dispensary and looked at me. She said I was humming. I was, apparently, the thing she hums from the choir, and worse than she does. The snow had settled overnight to a hand's depth and the lane was white and silent. The morning list was short: a sprained wrist from a sledge and a baby with nappy rash. Sanna said, 'The schoolmaster walked someone home last night. Frau Gruber saw.'
memories.did: I said Frau Gruber should have her eyes tested and I would do it free. Sanna snorted. I strapped the sprained wrist in a figure of eight and gave the baby's mother zinc ointment and told her to leave the nappy off by the stove as long as she could stand the mess. Between them I found I had written 'Teo' in the margin of the day book and scratched it out so hard the nib went through. Sanna saw that too. I told her to boil something.

memories.experienced: Lotte came at eleven while Mira was at a school friend's. She said she had something of mine, and put mother's garnet brooch on the examining couch between us. She said she had kept it nine years, sewn into the lining of her coat so Friedrich would not sell it. Then she said, 'You made me the villain of that will. Mother gave it to me because you were never home.' And I heard myself say, 'I was never home because I was paying for her doctors.'
memories.did: I did not pick it up. I said she had let me stand in that solicitor's office in Graz and be told I was the daughter who had not deserved a keepsake, and she had not said one word. She said she had been twenty-two and frightened. I said I had been twenty-nine and frightened, and we had both been cowards in the same room. I said it far too loudly. Sanna put her head round the door and went away again. I sat down on the couch because my legs wanted me to.

memories.experienced: Lotte sat down next to me with the brooch between us and started to cry, and then said, through it, that mother had worn the thing crooked every Sunday of her life and that neither of us had ever told her. I laughed, a horrible honk, and then Lotte was laughing too, and crying, and so was I. She said, 'Nine years over a pin that doesn't even close properly.' The clasp, when I finally picked it up, did not close properly.
memories.did: I held it to the window. One garnet was missing from the setting, the third on the left; Lotte said it had gone in the city and she had never had the money to replace it. I pinned it on her collar, crooked, on purpose. She tried to give it to me and I said no, keep it for Mira, that is what mother would have wanted if she had ever thought about anything past Sunday. We sat there until the kettle Sanna had put on quietly began to scream.

memories.experienced: In the quiet after dinner I took the hospital letter out of the desk drawer. The city was offering the assistant surgeon's post, two hundred and eighty crowns a month, rooms, a pension, and wanted an answer within six weeks, of which nearly three were gone. Out of the window the snow was blue under the lamp and I could hear Mira's laugh from the lane where Lotte was fetching her. The well was shut. The fever was nearly done. Teo had chalk on his sleeve.
