memories.did: I read the letter through once properly, then got out a sheet of paper and wrote 'Dear Sirs' and nothing else. I knew I was not going; I think I had known for weeks. But I did not write the refusal, because writing it makes it a thing I cannot take back, and I am a coward about closed doors. I folded the blank sheet into the letter and put both back in the drawer and went down to let Lotte and Mira in.

memories.experienced: Lotte and Mira came up for cocoa. Mira had built a snow doctor in the Gruber yard with two coal eyes and my old stethoscope drawn on with a stick, and she wanted me to go and see it before it melted. Lotte was wearing the brooch, still crooked. She said the Hart was charging her extra for coal now that it was cold. Mira asked whether the doctor's house had a room nobody used, and whose it was.
memories.did: I went out in my slippers to see the snow doctor and said he looked better qualified than Brenner, which Mira did not understand and Lotte did. I told Mira the back room over the dispensary was full of old boxes and nobody's, for now. Lotte gave me a look and said nothing. I made the cocoa with the good milk and let Mira stir it. When they left I stood in the hall and counted the boxes in the back room in my head.

memories.experienced: Late in the evening the orderly's boy brought the day's chart from the camp: five men in the fever bunkhouse, no new case in four days, three to be discharged in the morning. Twenty-six cases since the first on the eighteenth of October, one death. From the window the lamp at the portal was lit again for the night shift. I thought of Voss's hat and the green book, and that Hale had not come by since Thursday.
memories.did: I opened my casebook to a clean page and wrote the fever up in full: twenty-six cases, one death, Pavel Hruby, the navvy; source the upper camp well, fouled by water from the 1891 galleries after the tunnel drainage broke through; well closed the fifth of November on the mayor's order; last new case the seventh. I wrote 'ended' and underlined it. Then I added a line underneath, 'but the tunnel is still digging into the old workings, and I do not trust the air there either,' and blotted it and went to bed.

memories.experienced: Monday morning brought frost on the inside of the waiting-room window and three patients before eight. Frau Holle had sprained her wrist hauling a milk churn and swore it was broken. It was not. A carter's boy had a cough that sounded worse than it was. Sanna had the kettle on and told me the coal man wanted paying by Friday, and that she had counted only fourteen clean towels in the press, not the twenty I kept telling her we had.
memories.did: I strapped Frau Holle's wrist with a crepe bandage and told her, "Not broken. Stop carrying churns for a week or it will be." I listened to the carter's boy's chest front and back, gave him honey and linctus and sent him home. I told Sanna to put the coal man off until the twentieth. Then I counted the towels myself, got fourteen, and conceded the point with bad grace. She wrote it on her slate and underlined it twice.

memories.experienced: Just before noon Anton Reis came in, not for his old hand, which has healed to a shiny pink, but to sit on my bench and say it quietly. The heading smelled of gas, he said -- sweet and heavy, like rotten apples, since Saturday. "The lamps show nothing, doctor. Not a flicker in the flame. Every lamp on the shift." He said Stoll had told the men it was the powder smoke hanging and to get on. He had a headache that had not lifted in two days.
memories.did: I checked his pupils and his pulse, which were fine, and asked him exactly where in the heading: the last forty feet, he said, near the face on the left side. I said, "You remember what your own lamp looked like when you gave it me." He said he did. I asked him not to go in tomorrow. He said a man who does not go in does not get paid. I wrote the words "rotten apples, since Sat., all lamps" on a card and put it in my pocket.

memories.experienced: At one I went to Brandt's for bread because there was none upstairs. The shop smelled of caraway and the window was steamed. Otto Brandt said Mila had slept through three nights in a row now that the cold had turned dry, and Mila herself came out from the back with flour to the elbows to tell me she had not coughed at all at school. She has put on weight. Her cheeks were pink from the ovens, not from fever.
memories.did: I bought a rye loaf and two rolls for forty heller and made Mila breathe in and out for me at the counter, which she thinks is a game. Her chest was clear on both sides, no crackle at the bases. I told Otto to keep her in wool vests until April whatever she says. He tried to give me the rolls for nothing and I put the coins on the counter anyway. I ate one roll walking back, thinking about sweet smells and lamps that do not flicker.

memories.experienced: In the evening the clinic was quiet except for the stove ticking. The safety lamp Anton gave me in October was still locked in the dispensary press where I put it, the gauze with its opened and re-crimped seam. I took it out and held it to the lamplight and could see the slack in the mesh. My casebook was open at his page from the first week, the burned hand, and at the back flyleaf where I wrote down, in ship's shorthand, that the readings came out the same every shift.
memories.did: I copied Anton's card into the casebook under today's date, word for word, with the time: 11.50. I added a line: "Headache 2 days, no other signs. Advised not to enter." I wrote out, on a separate sheet, what I would say to Voss and Stoll tomorrow and crossed half of it out because it sounded like pleading. I decided to go up at eight before the day shift changed. I set the lamp in my bag so I would not lose my nerve and leave it behind.

memories.experienced: The contractor's office by the portal was a timber hut with a map of the ridge pinned over the stove. Voss was pleasant. He offered coffee. Stoll stood by the door with his arms folded. I said the men smelled gas at the face. Voss said the readings were clear and Stoll opened the gas log on the table and turned it round for me: every shift this week, '0.4', the same hand, the same ink. Voss said, "Doctor, I will not stop a heading because a shot-firer has a headache."
memories.did: I put Anton's lamp on the table beside the log and showed them the re-crimped seam. I said, "A lamp like this would read nil in a room full of gas. Clear the heading and air it for a day. One day." Voss said the lamp proved nothing about his lamps. Stoll said I should mind my bandages. I said, "If anyone dies in there I will say in front of whoever asks that I stood in this hut on the thirteenth and told you." Voss said, still smiling, "Noted." I took the lamp back and left.

memories.experienced: I found Inspector Hale in the back parlour of the Hart, eating eggs with his grey coat over the chair. He listened without interrupting, which is rare in this town. He said he believed me. He also said he had asked Voss twice for the foreman's working book and been shown the same clean one I had just seen, and that without the second book in his hand he could order an inspection of the ventilation but not a stoppage. He could not come up before Thursday; the district office had him in Brunnau Wednesday.
memories.did: I told him the time, the words, the lamp, and that Anton had said 'rotten apples'. He wrote it in his own notebook in pencil. I asked him outright to order the heading cleared. He said, "On what paper, Doctor?" I said, "On my say-so and a dead canary if you like." He did not laugh. He promised to telegraph the district from the station this afternoon asking for authority. I said Thursday might be late. He said he knew. I paid for his coffee because I was too angry to let him pay for mine.

memories.experienced: The afternoon was ordinary, which helped. The Wenger twins, four, both had red ears and fevers from the same cold. Old Herr Pichler's gout had flared in the right big toe after his son's name day and he wanted something for it that was not 'less wine'. A woman from the upper farms came in with a sickle cut across her palm, clean and not deep. Sanna said it had begun to sleet.
memories.did: I looked in four ears with the otoscope and prescribed warm oil and patience. I told Herr Pichler, "Less wine," and gave him colchicum anyway with a strict note on the dose. I put six stitches in the sickle cut, silk, and told the woman to come back Saturday to have them looked at. I wrote them all in the day book. Sanna and I ate bread and dripping at five standing up in the dispensary.

memories.experienced: Teodor came at seven with a jar of the plum jam his landlady makes and a stack of arithmetic slates he was meant to be marking. He said Mira had got every sum right and then drawn a horse on the back of the slate. When I told him about Voss he went quiet and then said the older boys at school had been repeating that the tunnel 'stinks at the end now'. He said, "Be careful, Ines. That man smiles like a bank."
memories.did: I made tea and we sat at my kitchen table upstairs and I told him the whole morning, the log, the lamp, 'Noted'. He marked slates while I talked and let me finish. I said, "I'm not careful, I'm right, which is worse." He laughed. When he left at half nine he kissed me at the top of the stairs and I stood there longer than necessary afterwards. I did not know what to call what we are, and I did not want to decide tonight.

memories.experienced: It sleeted all morning. At Grete's the bell over the door sounded thin. She had the pharmacy ledger open on the counter, as always, and ran her finger down my page without being asked. She said I had been in twice this week already. When I asked for carbolic, two pounds of lint, oiled silk and every jar of picric dressing she had, she raised an eyebrow and asked if I was expecting a war.
memories.did: I said, "Something like it." I took four jars of picric, the lint, the silk, a bottle of carbolic and a quarter of morphia, and told her to put it on my account. She wrote it in, the total now two hundred and eighty-four crowns, and turned the book so I could see the figure. I said I would pay something at the end of the month and meant it, roughly. I carried it home under my coat and stacked it on the burn shelf, telling myself I was being dramatic.

memories.experienced: After school let out I went to the Hart. Lotte was darning Mira's stockings by the window of their room and Mira was lying on the bed with a book about birds. Mira showed me a pressed gentian she had found by the schoolhouse wall and said it was the exact blue of the lamp glass in the church porch. Lotte said the landlord had raised the rate by a crown a week for the winter. The room smelled of wet wool drying on the rail.
memories.did: I sat on the end of the bed and let Mira teach me a card game called Sevens, which she cheats at openly. I lost three times. I said the porch glass was greener than that, and Mira said, "Not when the sun's behind it," and I did not argue. I told Lotte I would pay the extra crown. She said no. We left it at no for now. I did not mention the tunnel.

memories.experienced: Father Kurz caught me outside St. Veit's gate under his black umbrella. He told me, as if it were weather, that Mayor Dahl had given Herr Voss dinner at the Hart on Sunday, roast goose, and that the mayor had said at table the tunnel would break through to the south side by Easter if 'the nervous ones' left the engineers alone. He said he had also heard I had been up at the contractor's hut. He asked, kindly, whether I was sleeping.
memories.did: I said, "Who are the nervous ones, Father?" He said he supposed I was one of them. I said a priest ought to be nervous about men dying without warning. He patted my arm and said he would pray for the tunnel and for my temper, in that order. I thanked him for the goose report, which I meant, and walked home in the sleet the long way, past the station, so I would not have to talk to anyone else.

memories.experienced: At midnight I was still at my desk. The only sounds were the sleet on the roof and the night shift's compressor thumping faintly up at the portal. The letter from the city hospital lay on the desk where I had taken it out again, unanswered for three weeks. My casebook was open at yesterday's page. I kept seeing Stoll turning the gas log round for me to read, '0.4', '0.4', '0.4'.
memories.did: I wrote a formal letter to Konrad Voss, chief engineer: that on the 12th a shot-firer reported the odour of firedamp at the face, that safety lamps in use may be defective, that I requested the heading be cleared and ventilated, signed Dr. I. Calder, 12.20 a.m. I made two fair copies, one for Inspector Hale and one pinned into the casebook. I put the hospital letter back in the drawer, not the stove. I went to bed at two and did not sleep.

memories.experienced: Thursday began like any day. A navvy's wife from the camp brought her baby, six weeks, screaming with colic, red in the face and pulling his knees up. She had walked down in the dark. Sanna had posted my letter to Voss by the camp boy at half seven. The sleet had stopped and there was sun on the snow for the first time all week, so bright it hurt.
memories.did: I undressed the baby on the warm towel by the stove, felt his belly, soft, no mass, nothing twisted. I showed the mother how to hold him face down along her forearm and rub his back, and he stopped crying within three minutes, which made me look far cleverer than I am. I gave her dill water and told her to feed him less at a time. She said, "You're not as frightening as they say," and I said nobody is.

memories.experienced: At eleven forty I was writing up the colic baby when the windows jumped in their frames. It was not loud so much as heavy, a thump I felt in my chest and the soles of my feet, and a second later the cups rattled on the dispensary shelf. Then the bell at the portal began, the long ringing that means men are inside. Sanna came in from the yard white as the snow and said, "The tunnel."
memories.did: I said, "Burn bag. All the picric, all the lint, the morphia, the oiled silk." We filled two bags in under four minutes; I had stacked the shelf on Wednesday and I thanked God for my own dramatics. I told Sanna to lock the door and put a note on it saying where we were. We ran up the portal road, the bags banging our hips, and I kept thinking one thing over and over: I told him on Tuesday. I told him. It took us eighteen minutes to climb.

memories.experienced: At the portal smoke was still rolling out along the roof of the bore and men were coughing on their knees in the snow. They carried the first four out on planks. Jakob Stoll was the second one; he had been at the face checking the round before firing, they said, and he was dead, his face and chest burned and his neck at a wrong angle where the blast had thrown him. Anton was the third, alive, screaming, both forearms and the left side of his face burned raw.
memories.did: I knelt by Stoll, felt for a pulse I knew was not there, and said to the gang, "He's gone. Cover him." I moved on to Anton, cut his sleeves off, poured the picric over his arms and face and gave him a quarter grain of morphia. I told two men to hold a tarpaulin over him against the wind. Voss came out of the hut with no coat on and stood looking at Stoll's body. I said to him, loud, "Get every man out of that heading. Now." This time he did it.

memories.experienced: The night went on in lantern light in the portal store, which they cleared for me. The other three burned were Karl Ebner, a boy called Fritzi Brook, and an older miner named Lorenz with burns to both legs. Dr. Brenner came up from the camp at about two in the morning with his own bag. He did not say ague this time. He said, "Tell me what you want me to do." Grete had sent up her boy with a sack of lint and castor oil and a note saying 'no charge, don't argue'.
memories.did: I set Brenner to Lorenz's legs and took Fritzi, whose hands were the worst after Anton's. Every hour I went back to Anton, checked his breathing, his pulse, gave him water with salt and sugar by the spoon. At four his pulse went thin and fast and I thought I was losing him; I sat and held the cup and told him about the colic baby to keep him listening. I did not sit down otherwise. By dawn I had used all four jars of picric and every inch of the lint.

memories.experienced: At first light Anton opened his good eye and knew me. His voice was cracked from the smoke. He said, "The lamps showed nothing, doctor. Right up to it. Nothing." His pulse had steadied. Inspector Hale came up the road just after seven with Emil Ott, who had wired the district about the explosion at noon and met him off the first train. Hale stood in the store doorway and looked at the four men on the floor and asked me which book the foreman had been writing in last.
memories.did: I told Anton he was going to live, which I had not known until I said it. I told Hale, "The clean one's in Voss's hut. The other one Stoll kept on him or where he slept. Find it before somebody burns it." I gave Hale the fair copy of my letter from Wednesday night. He read it standing and put it inside his coat. Then I went outside and was sick into the snow behind the store, and Sanna held my hair back like I was a patient.

memories.experienced: By nine the four burned men were down at the clinic on stretchers carried by their own gang, Anton in the back room by himself because his face needed the dark. I slept two hours in my clothes upstairs and woke with my hands still smelling of picric. Sanna had changed all four sets of dressings alone and wrote each one up on the slate with the time. Fritzi had asked for his mother, who lives in Silesia.
memories.did: I checked every dressing Sanna had done and could not find a thing wrong with any of them, and told her so, which made her cry for a moment by the sink. I wrote all four men into the casebook: names, burns by area, fluids, morphia doses, times. For Anton I wrote "approx. one-fifth of body, face, both forearms, left eye closed but lid intact". I wrote a card for Fritzi's mother for Ott to send. I ate nothing until two.

memories.experienced: At three Lotte came up the clinic stairs with a pot of barley soup wrapped in a shawl, and Mira behind her carrying a bundle of torn sheets from the Hart's landlady for bandages. Lotte said the whole town had heard the bang; they had felt it in the Hart's dining room and a mirror cracked. Mira stood very close to my chair and asked if the men with no faces would get their faces back.
memories.did: I said, "Their faces are there, love, only burned. Skin grows back if we keep it clean." She thought about it and then asked if she could roll the bandages, so I showed her how to tear the sheets in three-inch strips and roll them tight, and she did forty before supper and counted them out loud. Lotte washed every basin in the dispensary without asking and then made me eat two bowls of soup while she watched. I let her.

memories.experienced: Mayor Dahl came at six in his good overcoat and did not take it off. He said the town grieved for Stoll, and that the company would pay the burned men's wages in full while they healed. He said, choosing his words, that it would help everyone if the doctor did not 'speculate in public' before the railway's inquiry, and that accidents happen in every tunnel in Europe. He glanced at the burn shelf, empty now, and did not ask about the men.
memories.did: I said, "It was not an accident, Herr Mayor, it was a warning ignored. I have it in writing with the date." He said he was sure I meant well. I said I meant accurately. I told him the men would be paid their wages or I would tell the inquiry that too. He asked whether I intended to stay on in Kessel Pass after all this, and I said that was my business. I showed him out myself and bolted the door after him.

memories.experienced: Teodor came when the lamps were lit. He had kept the school closed today, the day after the bang, because the children were frightened and three of them had fathers on the shift. He did not say anything clever. He took the kettle out of my hands and sat me down. When he asked if I had eaten I said Lotte had fed me and he said, "Good. Your sister is a sensible woman."
memories.did: I told him Stoll was dead and that I had said to his face two days before that someone would be. Then I cried, for the first time since the portal, with my face in his coat for perhaps five minutes, badly. He did not tell me it was not my fault, which is why I could stop. At ten he went to sit with Anton so I could sleep an hour, and read to him from a book of Alpine birds because it was the only book on my shelf that wasn't medicine.

memories.experienced: Saturday morning I still had a clinic to run. Frau Wenger's eldest daughter-in-law, eight months gone and swollen at the ankles, came for her check. The woman with the sickle cut came back as I had told her to; the stitches were clean and dry. Sanna had put the kettle on at six and swept the snow from the step. The whole waiting room was talking about the funeral at ten.
memories.did: I measured the pregnant woman's belly with the tape, twenty-nine inches, heard the baby's heart at one-forty on the left, and checked her ankles and her urine for albumin, which was clear. I told her feet up after dinner and no salt pork. I took the sickle stitches out myself, all six, and bound the palm lightly. At nine-thirty I changed out of my apron and into my one black dress and left Sanna in charge of the four men.

memories.experienced: The church was full: the whole tunnel gang in their Sunday coats, the camp wives, the mayor. Stoll's sister had come up from Innsbruck on the early train. Father Kurz said Stoll had been a hard worker and a faithful man, which was half true. Voss stood in the second pew in black and bowed his head at the right places. At the graveside he looked across the hole at me once and then away. On my way out I passed the little stone by the east wall: Petr Anko, aged eleven.
memories.did: I stood at the back through the Mass and sang nothing. At the grave I threw my handful of earth like everyone else and said to Stoll's sister, "I was with him at the end. It was quick." I did not tell her I had warned him. When Voss looked at me I held his eye until he dropped it. At the east wall I stopped at Petr's stone for longer than I meant to, and touched the top of it, which I have never let myself do, and walked out through the lych-gate before anyone could speak to me.

memories.experienced: At one Hale came to fetch me; he wanted a witness who was not the company's. We walked up to the camp to the foreman's hut behind bunkhouse two. Stoll's things were in a tin trunk. Under the straw mattress, wrapped in oilcloth, was a second gas log, bound in green cloth. Hale opened both books on the table: the same dates, the same shifts, but in the hidden one the readings at the face for the last nine days were written as 'heavy', '2 per cent', 'lamp capped blue'.
memories.did: I read the entry for Tuesday, the day I stood in Voss's hut: 'Face -- 2½ %, men complaining, K.V. says carry on.' I read it aloud so Hale's constable would hear. Voss arrived at the hut door while we were wrapping the book and said it was a dead man's scribble and company property. Hale said, "It is evidence now, Herr Voss," and signed a receipt for it on the spot. I initialled the receipt as witness at 1.40. I did not say anything to Voss. I did not need to.

memories.experienced: In the late afternoon I changed Anton's dressings. The burns on his forearms were weeping but clean, no smell of infection, and the new skin was pinking at the edges. The left eye opened today for the first time, bloodshot but seeing. He asked about the funeral. He said Stoll had three children in Linz he sent money to, and that Stoll had shouted at him in the heading on Monday to stop whining about the air.
memories.did: I soaked the old lint off with warm saline so it wouldn't tear, dressed both arms with fresh picric and oiled silk, and tested his left eye with a candle; he followed it. I told him Hale had the other book now. He said, "Then Stoll wrote it down. He knew," and turned his face to the wall. I sat with him ten minutes and said nothing. I wrote in the casebook: 'Day 3. Eye sighted. No sepsis. Spirits low.'

memories.experienced: Evening, and the thaw had started: water ran from the eaves all night and the gutters overflowed onto the step. Sanna had gone home at seven. The four men were asleep. I sat by the stove in the kitchen upstairs with a mending basket I never get to the bottom of. The city hospital letter was in the drawer where I put it on Wednesday, and every time I reached for thread I saw its corner.
memories.did: I sewed a button on my grey cardigan and darned one stocking badly. I took the hospital letter out and read it again, the salary, the surgical wing, 'a colleague of your experience', and asked myself whether I would have seen this coming with better lamps and a whole hospital behind me, and knew I had seen it coming anyway. I put the letter back in the drawer. I went down twice in the night to look at the men. Lorenz asked for water; nobody else woke.

memories.experienced: Sunday, and a boy called Kaspar Moll was brought in by his grandmother at nine with a goat bite on his calf. He had been feeding it through the fence and it had decided he was the feed. The bite was a neat crescent, not deep, but dirty. His grandmother talked the whole time about the goat's temper. Church bells were going across the square for the late Mass.
memories.did: I cleaned the bite with carbolic while Kaspar yelled, trimmed a flap of skin, and left it open with a light dressing because goats are filthy. I told the grandmother to keep it dry and bring him back Tuesday, and to sell the goat. She said the goat was worth more than the boy. I gave Kaspar a barley sugar from the jar I keep for children and he stopped crying at once, the little fraud. I wrote him in the day book.

memories.experienced: At eleven Grete came in person, which she never does, carrying a basket: more lint, a bottle of castor oil, zinc ointment and two jars of picric she had sent to Brunnau for. She said the pharmacy ledger could 'sit closed' until after the inquiry and she did not want to hear the word account from me until then. She looked into the back room at Anton and her mouth went thin. She said Voss's clerk had been in yesterday trying to buy up every burn dressing in town for the company.
memories.did: I said, "Grete, I owe you nearly three hundred crowns." She said, "Two hundred and eighty-four. I can count. We'll talk after." I thanked her properly, which I find hard, and she told me to stop it. I put the jars on the burn shelf. I asked what she had told Voss's clerk and she said, "That I was out." I laughed for the first time in three days. I made her coffee and she drank it standing and left.

memories.experienced: In the afternoon Sanna sent me out: go for a walk, she said, you are frightening the patients. I walked without deciding where and found myself on Mill Lane in front of the old clinic. The shutters were grey and the four screw holes where my brass plate hung were full of moss. The side door was not locked, only swollen. Inside it smelled of damp plaster and mice. The operating room was as it had been: the high window, the iron table stripped to its frame, a ring on the floorboards where the basin stand stood.
memories.did: I had not walked down Mill Lane in six years without looking the other way. I shouldered the side door open and went in and sat on the one chair in the operating room for, by my watch, fifty minutes. I put my hand on the cold table where Petr lay. I said his name out loud once. I thought: my notes from that year are all in the old volumes of the casebook, and I have never once reread them, and I should. I pulled the door shut behind me when I left.

memories.experienced: Teodor was sitting on the clinic step when I came back at dusk, with his collar up, because Sanna had told him where I had gone, or at least which way. He had a note for me that Hale had left at the door: the railway inquiry would sit on Wednesday at nine in the station waiting room, and I was called as a witness, and should bring 'all relevant notes'. The snow along the lane had turned to slush.
memories.did: I sat down on the step beside him and said, "I sat in it. The old operating room. Fifty minutes." He asked how it was. I said, "Smaller than I remember." He put his arm round me and did not ask anything else. I read Hale's note twice and said I would bring the whole casebook, every volume, back to the first year. He said he would help me carry them. We went in and I heated the soup Lotte had left.

memories.experienced: Anton was still in the back room when I came down at seven, propped on two pillows, the burns on his forearms weeping less than yesterday. Sanna had already boiled the linen and laid out the picric. The skin on his right hand, the old burned one, had come through a second time and was pink at the edges. He told me he had dreamed of the heading again and woken smelling it. The blast was four days gone and the room still smelled of singed wool from his coat, which Sanna refused to throw out.
memories.did: I cut the old dressings off with the curved scissors, soaked the stuck patches with warm saline, and counted: no new blisters, no green, no smell of rot. I told Anton, "You will keep the hand, and you will hate me for the next fortnight." I laid fresh lint soaked in picric under oiled silk, bandaged both arms to the elbow, and wrote the state of each burn in my casebook with the time, 7.40. I told Sanna to burn the coat. She said she would wash it instead. I let her win.

memories.experienced: Inspector Hale came at half past ten with his grey coat dark from the drizzle. He said the three men from the railway board had come up on the morning train and the inquiry would sit on Wednesday as his note said, from nine o'clock, in the station waiting room, because it was the only room in town with enough chairs. He said he would present both gas logs, the one Stoll showed him and the green one Stoll kept under his mattress. He wanted me to bring my casebook, Anton's lamp, and my notes on the well.
memories.did: I made him tea he did not drink. I said, "You want a doctor who writes everything down. You have one." I fetched the lamp from the dispensary press, where it had sat locked away since the night Anton brought it, wrapped it in a clean tea towel, and showed him again where the gauze had been opened and crimped back with pliers. He asked me not to clean it. I promised. I wrote on a card: Wed., 9 o'clock, waiting room, casebook, lamp, well samples, and pinned it over my desk.

memories.experienced: At the bakery the queue went out the door because of the rain, everybody wanting warm bread. Otto Brandt had flour to his elbows and shouted that his Mila had not coughed at night for six nights running. Mila was sitting on a flour sack behind the counter eating the end of a plait loaf. When I listened to her back with the stethoscope under her jumper, the crackle at the right base I had heard all autumn had not come back. She breathed like any nine-year-old.
memories.did: I bought two rye loaves and a bag of rolls, and Otto would not take my coins, so I left them on the scale. I made Mila breathe in and out ten times and count them aloud. I told Otto, "Keep her out of the flour dust in the mornings and keep doing whatever you are doing." He said he was doing nothing. I said that was often the best medicine and he should not tell anyone I said so.

memories.experienced: After supper I took my casebook to the kitchen table with the lamp turned up. The fever pages were worse to read than to write. Eleven cases in the first ten days, Pavel Hruby who died on the twenty-fourth, the camp plan with the upper well circled in red, my note from the upper well on the second of November: cloudy, metallic, smells of the mine. My handwriting got smaller the more frightened I had been. The clock downstairs struck one before I had finished.
memories.did: I copied every fever case onto a single sheet in order of date, with bunkhouse, well, and outcome, so the board could see the cluster at a glance. Twenty-six cases, one death, the last two days after the well was closed on the fifth of November and none since. I marked the pages for the lamp and the explosion with torn strips of newspaper. I said out loud to the empty kitchen, "Read it like a stranger would," and then went back to the first volume to check nothing earlier contradicted me.

memories.experienced: Morning surgery was ordinary and I was grateful for it. The carter's wife came in with her heartburn, worse since the cold, and a list of everything she had eaten that week. Then an old man with a split thumbnail from his woodpile, then two children with the same chesty cough from the same classroom. The rain had turned to sleet and the waiting room floor was a slurry of melted mud that Sanna kept mopping and muttering at.
memories.did: I gave the carter's wife bicarbonate and the old lecture about pickled herring, which she recited along with me, laughing, and promised to give up the herring on the same day her husband gave up his pipe, which is to say never. I trimmed and dressed the thumbnail. For the children I wrote steam, honey, and a note for their mother. I charged the carter's wife nothing and the old man half a crown.

memories.experienced: Going back through the first volume for the inquiry, I reached the Anko pages. Six years ago, eight days before the operation, in my own hand: Petr A., 11 yrs. Soft systolic murmur, left sternal border. Tires on the stairs. Lips dusky after running, per mother. Query -- recheck. I never rechecked. Then the admission for the bowel, the operation, and the line I had read a hundred times in my head: heart failed under chloroform, could not be restarted. I had never once read the page before it.
memories.did: I sat very still and read it four times. Then I got the old cardiology text off the top shelf and read the chapter on congenital defects, the ones with a hole between the chambers, children who tire, who go blue. No surgeon alive then, or now, could have closed it. I said, "It wasn't the knife," and then, because that was too easy, "You wrote it down and didn't look." I put a strip of newspaper at the page and closed the book.

memories.experienced: Teo was wiping the blackboard when I came into the schoolhouse after lessons, chalk dust on his sleeves. He saw my face and put the rag down without asking. I told him about the murmur. He listened the way he does, not nodding, and when I stopped he said, "So you did see it coming. You just couldn't have stopped it." He said that was not the same crime. The stove ticked. Mira's drawing of the schoolhouse with every window lit was pinned by the window.
memories.did: I opened the casebook on a pupil's desk too small for me and showed him the line, my finger under 'recheck'. I said, "Six years I have been carrying the wrong stone." He asked what I would do. I said I thought I owed Marta Anko the page, whether she wanted it or not. He did not tell me not to. I let him hold my hand across the little desk for longer than a friend would, and I did not take it back.

memories.experienced: Supper with Lotte and Mira at the Hart: potato soup and sausage, Mira picking out the onions. Lotte said the innkeeper had put the room up to four crowns a week now the tunnel men were back in town and paying in cash. She said it lightly, the way she says things that frighten her. Mira was telling me about a fox she saw behind the school, and for the first time she did not look at her mother before answering my question.
memories.did: I asked Mira what colour the fox was and whether it had a white tip on its tail; she said yes, like a paintbrush. Then I said to Lotte, before I could make it sensible, "There are two back rooms upstairs that nobody uses but the mice. Take them." Lotte said she would think. I said the mice would not charge four crowns. Mira said she was not afraid of mice. I paid for the soup and walked them to the stairs.

memories.experienced: Just after midnight a boy from the camp hammered on the door: a navvy had fallen down the bunkhouse steps drunk and split his scalp. Down at the bunkhouses the men were quiet, card games instead of fights, washing frozen stiff on the lines. The man had a two-inch cut over his crown, bleeding the way scalps do, like murder, and he was singing a song about a girl from Linz.
memories.did: I washed the cut in a tin basin, shaved round it with his mate's razor, and put in five silk stitches while two men held his head and joined in the song. I told him, "If you fall again tonight, fall on your face; it's uglier already." They laughed; he did not understand. I wrote his name, Matthias Pohl, and the five stitches on the back of my hand because the casebook was at home, and walked back up the hill alone.

memories.experienced: The station waiting room at quarter to nine smelled of wet coats and coal. Emil Ott had pushed the benches into rows and set a trestle table under the timetable board for the three men from the railway board, who sat with their hats on the table in a line. The room was full: navvies at the back, Father Kurz, the mayor in his fur collar. Voss sat at the front with a lawyer in a good suit and did not turn round.
memories.did: I carried my casebook, this year's volume and the first, tied with string, and the lamp still in its tea towel. Ott found me a chair by the stove and whispered that he had never seen so many people in there, not even for the Emperor's train. I said, "Then sell them tickets." I laid the books on my knees, checked the newspaper markers were all still in place, and made myself breathe slowly the way I tell patients to.

memories.experienced: They called me at ten past ten. The chairman, a thin man called Gerlach, asked about the injuries since spring and I read them from my casebook. Voss's lawyer asked whether a country doctor was qualified to judge a safety lamp, then read out Dr. Brenner's first report, which called the fever mountain ague and nothing to do with the tunnel. Brenner, sitting at the side, stood up unasked and said he had been wrong and that his second report said so. Someone at the back said, "Tell them, doctor," and was hushed.
memories.did: I unwrapped Anton's lamp and passed it up, and showed them where the gauze had been opened and re-crimped, the pliers' teeth marks still in the brass. I said, "A lamp that cannot see gas is a lie with a wick in it." Then the fever sheet: twenty-six cases, the upper well, the drainage into the old galleries, the last case two days after the well was shut and none since. To the lawyer I said, "Ague does not stop when you change the water." Gerlach wrote that down.

memories.experienced: After the midday break Hale put two books on the trestle, side by side. In the black one Stoll had shown him every shift for nine weeks the firedamp read point four, the same pencil, the same hand. In the green one from under Stoll's mattress the readings climbed: one and a half, two, two and a half in the last week before the blast. Anton gave evidence with his arms bandaged, saying the heading stank for a week and the lamps showed nothing.
memories.did: I watched Voss while Hale read the numbers aloud, and Voss looked at his fingernails. When Anton stumbled over a date I did not help him, because they had told me not to, but I nodded when he looked at me. Afterwards I told Hale, "You held on to that green book like a man holding a baby." He said he had slept with it under his pillow. I wrote the three readings in my own book so I would never have to trust anyone's copy.

memories.experienced: At half past five the board came back from the stationmaster's office. Gerlach read the finding: the chief engineer had knowingly worked the heading on false readings; Konrad Voss was dismissed from the contractor's service with immediate effect and handed to the district police on a charge of criminal negligence causing death. Two constables from Grauberg stood up by the door. Mayor Dahl said the tunnel must not stop for one man. Nobody answered him.
memories.did: I did not clap when the navvies did. I watched Voss walk out between the constables, still buttoning his gloves, and felt nothing I could name. Outside on the platform Hale shook my hand and said, "Your book did more than mine." I said, "Mine only counted the dead; yours explained them." The mayor passed us without a word. I walked home in the dark and slept in my clothes on top of the blanket.

memories.experienced: I slept until nine, which I have not done since the navy. Sanna had opened the surgery without me and seen three patients: a sprain, a boil, and Frau Keller's bad nerves, which she said she had treated with tea and letting Frau Keller talk. Rain on the skylight. At ten a mother brought in her little boy screaming with earache, one ear red and bulging, holding his head sideways against her coat.
memories.did: I looked in the ear with the speculum and said, "That drum's about to go on its own." I put warm oil drops in, gave the mother a sachet of fever powder for the night and told her if it burst and ran she was not to panic, it would ease. I told Sanna, "You should charge for the nerves." She said Frau Keller paid in eggs. I ate two of them, boiled, at the dispensary bench.

memories.experienced: Marta Anko lives in the end house on Tanner's Row, green door, a boot-scraper shaped like a hedgehog. I stood on the step long enough to be seen from the window. When she opened the door she was smaller than I remembered, grey all through now, a dish cloth in her hand. She looked at me, and at the casebook under my arm, and said, "I heard what you said at the station." Then, after a long time, "Come in, then."
memories.did: I had rehearsed a speech and said none of it. I said, "I found something in my notes about Petr. You should see it, and then you can put me out." She stood back from the door. I wiped my boots on the hedgehog, twice, and went into her kitchen, and stood by the table until she told me to sit, because I did not think I had the right.

memories.experienced: Marta read the page with her finger under each word. Then she told me what I had never asked: that Petr went blue at the lips when he was born, that the midwife said he'd grow out of it, that he never ran as far as the other boys. She said, "I hated you because it was easier than hating God." She asked if I still went to Mill Lane. Her kitchen smelled of caraway and the kettle hissed on and on.
memories.did: I told her plainly: a hole in the heart, most likely, that no surgeon could have mended; that the chloroform found the weakness; that I had written down the murmur and should have looked again, and I was sorry for that part, the part that was mine. I told her I had sat in the old operating room last week for an hour. She poured tea. We drank it without talking. When I left she said, "Come on his birthday. March the ninth." I said I would.

memories.experienced: St. Veit's was dark except for the red lamp and the rack of candles. Father Kurz came out of the vestry in his slippers and sat down in the pew in front of me, turned round, arm over the back. He already knew I had been to Tanner's Row; Frau Pichler from the post office had seen me go in and timed me, fifty minutes. He said Marta had lit a candle for Petr every Sunday for six years and never once let him say my name.
memories.did: I put ten heller in the box and lit one candle next to Marta's row, for the boy, and a second one because I felt like it, for Stoll, whom I had not liked. I told Kurz, "You gossip like a barber." He said it was a pastoral service. I did not tell him what the page said; it was Marta's to tell. I sat until the candles were half down and then went home to write up Anton.

memories.experienced: The letter from the city hospital had been in the desk drawer since the night before the blast, its corner curling. Mornings are quiet before seven; the only sounds were the stove and Sanna's key in the lock downstairs at ten to. The offer was still good: the assistant surgeon's post, a salary three times what Kessel Pass pays me in eggs and promises, a flat with a bathroom. I read it once more to be fair to it.
memories.did: I wrote on my good paper: Dear Professor Almer, I thank you for your offer and must decline it. My patients here have no one else, and I have lately learned how much I can see if I look. I signed it, blotted it, and addressed it. I told myself it was not because of Teo, which was only mostly true. I put the letter in my coat pocket and the offer itself in the stove, with the acceptance I had drafted in October and never sent, and watched them go.

memories.experienced: Emil Ott weighed the letter on the brass scale in the booking office and said it needed a twenty-heller stamp, city rate. He noticed the address, of course; he notices everything that passes through his hands. He said, "The hospital in the city. Going away, doctor?" The down mail went at 10.40 and he said it would be on the professor's desk the day after tomorrow. The waiting room was back to its benches, as if the inquiry had never sat.
memories.did: I paid for the stamp and licked it myself and said, "I'm telling them no, Emil, so you can stop composing the gossip." He looked disappointed and then pleased. I stood on the platform until the 10.40 came in, watched the mailbag go into the van, and felt as if I'd posted a piece of myself. Then I went to buy lamp oil, because the clinic was nearly out.

memories.experienced: Grete had her ledger open on the counter before I said a word. My page: two hundred and eighty-four crowns, eighty-three of it quinine and fever powders from the fever weeks, when she had given me credit because men were dying. She said the company had paid her for the camp's stock after the inquiry, through the mayor's office, embarrassed into it. Then she ran a ruler down the fever months and drew one line through them in red ink.
memories.did: I put forty crowns on the counter, all I had saved since the fever ended. I said, "What are you doing to my account?" She said, "The fever was the town's bill, not yours. You owe me for the rest: a hundred and sixty-one crowns." I argued, badly. She told me to go away before she changed her mind. I said, "Thank you, Grete," which I have never once said in that shop, and bought a tin of carbolic with cash.

memories.experienced: In the afternoon the carrier's lad fetched me to the stable yard behind the brewery: a mule driver had been kicked and his shoulder was out, the arm hanging dead and the man grey and swearing in two languages. The sleet had stopped and the sun came out weakly over the ridge, and the yard steamed. The mule stood in its stall looking entirely innocent.
memories.did: I laid him flat on a pile of sacks, put my stockinged foot in his armpit and pulled steady on his wrist, counting aloud to forty, until it went back with a clunk he felt in his teeth. I strapped the arm to his chest with his own belt and a scarf. I told him, "Stay away from the back end of that animal for a week." He gave me a bottle of plum brandy, which I took home for Sanna.

memories.experienced: Lotte came at dusk with Mira asleep on her shoulder and said, "Show me the mice." Upstairs the two back rooms smelled of dust and old apples; the bigger one has the window over the yard and a crack in the plaster shaped like Italy. Lotte walked round it twice with her lips moving. She said the Hart wanted the next week in advance on Monday. Then she said, very quietly, that Friedrich did not know this street existed.
memories.did: I held the candle while she paced the room out, four steps by five. I said the bed frame was sound and I would find a mattress, and Sanna's cousin had a chest of drawers going cheap. I said, "He can't find it. And if he did, he would find me first." She laughed at that, a real one. We agreed: they move in tomorrow, she pays nothing till she has work, and she does the Tuesday wash. We shook on it like men.

memories.experienced: Moving day. The Hart's porter loaded two trunks and a hatbox on the handcart and charged Lotte a crown for it. Mira insisted on carrying her own satchel and a jam jar with a sprig of heather from the school walk, and would not let anyone near the jar. The sun was out for once and the whole length of Kirchgasse was dripping off the eaves. People stared at us, Father Kurz waved from the church steps, and I did not mind.
memories.did: I pushed the cart myself up the hill from the inn because the porter was slow, and Lotte walked beside it with one hand on the top trunk in case it slid. I told Mira the jar would get the windowsill in the little room, the best spot. On the clinic stairs the bigger trunk stuck on the turn and I swore, and Mira said the word back to me, delighted, and Lotte said, "Well done, Ines."

memories.experienced: I was on my knees putting shelf paper in the washstand drawer when Mira came in holding a bar of her mother's lavender soap and asked, "Aunt Ines, where does the soap go?" She said it like she had been saying it for years. Then she stood waiting for an answer, not looking at me any differently, as if nothing had happened. Downstairs I could hear Lotte and Sanna arguing kindly about where the kettle lived.
memories.did: I said, "In the dish, beside the jug," and my voice came out wrong, so I pretended to cough. I showed her the dish, the chipped one with the blue rim. She put the soap in it and lined it up just so. I asked if she wanted the bed by the window or by the wall; she said window, for the fox. I finished the drawer and went and stood in the yard for a minute on my own.

memories.experienced: While we unpacked the second trunk Lotte took out a small box wrapped in a stocking and put it on the mantel in their room: mother's garnet brooch, the one we had been cruel to each other about for nine years and laughed about a fortnight ago. She said, "It belongs to the house, not to either of us. That's what the will should have said." The garnets were dull and needed cleaning. The clasp still did not shut.
memories.did: I picked it up and said, "It's uglier than I remembered." She said it was always ugly; mother had terrible taste. I said I'd mend the clasp with the fine forceps from the instrument tray, and did, there and then, with her holding the lamp. We put it on the mantel between Mira's heather jar and the clock. I did not say anything about the will. For once there was nothing to say.

memories.experienced: Just before eleven there was knocking on the surgery door, polite at first and then not. A young navvy from the new shift with his jaw swollen like a pear, a back molar rotten to the root, three days of not sleeping and a lot of schnapps poured on it that had done nothing but make him weepy. Upstairs a floorboard creaked; someone new was listening to the house now.
memories.did: I sat him in the chair under the lamp, gave him a swallow of the mule driver's plum brandy and a dab of cocaine solution on the gum, and pulled the molar with the forceps in one long turn. It came out whole with three roots. I gave it to him in a twist of paper, which they always want. I charged him a crown. I told him, "Salt water every hour, and no more schnapps in the hole."

memories.experienced: The Sunday stalls in the square were thin, the snow still banked along the fountain. I was buying eggs from the Huber woman, a dozen at forty heller, when Marta Anko came along the row with her basket. Six years she had turned away when she saw me. This time she stopped at the next stall, looked at me over the potatoes, and nodded once. That was all. The egg woman noticed and almost dropped my change.
memories.did: I nodded back and said, "Good morning, Frau Anko." She said, "Doctor," and went on to the cheeses. I did not follow her or say anything else, because a nod in the market is a large thing here and I did not want to make it smaller. I carried the eggs home very carefully, as though they were the thing that might break, and wrote the ninth of March on the kitchen calendar.

memories.experienced: Hale left on the noon train with a single valise and the two gas logs in a leather case chained to his wrist, which he said was theatrical but regulation. On the platform he told me Voss would be tried in the city in the spring, and that the contractor had sent a new engineer who would keep the gas book with an inspector's countersign every shift. Emil Ott blew his whistle as if it were a state occasion.
memories.did: I brought Hale a paper of Otto Brandt's rolls for the journey. I said, "When you inspect the next tunnel, take a doctor down it first." He said he'd put it in his report, and I believe he will. I shook his hand and then, because the grey coat was so sad, straightened his collar. I stood with Ott until the train was gone behind the ridge, then walked up past the tunnel portal, where the fans were running again.

memories.experienced: Teo called for me at five and we walked up the old mule path to the silver mine, the snow crusted and blue in the shade. The main adit is boarded now, and the new pump house the contractor built to keep the drainage out of the galleries was thumping away below it. By the entrance is the stone for the 1891 collapse, eleven names, moss in the letters. Teo read them aloud one by one, and the last was a boy of fourteen.
memories.did: I brushed the moss out of the boy's name with my glove. I told Teo that Father Kurz's map had those galleries running right under the heading, and that nearly all my fever cases had drunk this mountain's water. He said, "You look at a hill and see a patient." I said, "I look at a hill and see a hill. You're the patient." He laughed and took my arm for the steep bit, and neither of us let go after it flattened.

memories.end: at peace, tired in the good way
memories.experienced: On the spoil heap above the workings we could see the whole town: the station lamps, the camp stovepipes, St. Veit's, and my own window, where Lotte had put a lamp for us. The sun went down behind the ridge fast, the way it does in the pass. Teo asked if I had answered the city. When I told him, he said, "Good," and then, "I mean, for the town," and then gave up and kissed me, cold-nosed.
memories.did: I told him I'd posted the refusal on Friday on the 10.40 and burned the offer in my stove. I said, "I'm staying because this is where my notes are," which was a joke and not a joke. I kissed him back. We came down in the dark with his matches, slipping on the ice and holding on, and at the bottom of the path I pointed out Lotte's lamp and said, "That's home." He walked me all the way to the clinic door.
